# Circuit Synthesis for Variational Quantum Algorithms: The Depth of Algebra and Geometry Boris Tsvelikhovskiy
1,∗ 1_Department of Mathematics, University of California, Riverside, CA 92521, USA_ The analysis of Hamiltonian Variational Ansätze centers on three fundamental questions: which states are exactly reachable from a given initial state, what native control depth suffices for local and global synthesis, and whether a bounded circuit extension can expose a direction of decreasing cost at a suboptimal output. We address these challenges by leveraging the dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) associated with the circuits and the geometry of the initial state’s orbit under the action of the corresponding dynamical Lie group _G_. We prove that an initial state has a closed projective orbit whenever it is a nondegenerate eigenstate of a control Hamiltonian, without requiring the dynamical Lie group itself to be closed. Combined with asymptotic QAOA convergence, this guarantees exact, finite depth ground state preparation for architectures employing diagonal problem Hamiltonians and irreducible stoquastic mixers. We also show that an orbit of quadratic dimension can contain exponentially many mutually orthogonal optimal states, demonstrating how a small reachable manifold can accommodate a large family of solutions. We bound the number of native control exponentials required for local unitary synthesis and state preparation using DLA commutator filtration growth alongside reachable orbit dimensions. Complementing these local results, we construct global frameworks on invariant sectors equipped with full unitary or special unitary dynamical Lie algebras. These constructions yield explicit applications to Pauli-generated systems and constrained maximum independent set multi-angle QAOA circuits; specifically, we show that their native control costs are directly determined by commutator filtration depth and independent-set toggle-group geometry, respectively. Finally, if the dynamical Lie group is compact, the observable _HP_ generates an admissible evolution (\(iHP\in\text{g}\), where g is the DLA), and the projective orbit of the initial state contains a ground state ray of _HP_, then a bounded depth, identity-initialized circuit extension exhibits either first-order descent or negative curvature at every suboptimal circuit output. ### I. INTRODUCTION Variational circuits built from Hamiltonian evolutions employ a prescribed set of controls at every depth. For instance, the celebrated Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) employs a variational ansatz produced by alternating unitary evolutions generated by the exponentials of the problem and mixer Hamiltonians [12, 15]; related constructions appear throughout variational quantum algorithms (VQA) [8]. Although asymptotic convergence to the optimal eigenspace is established for suitable QAOA mixers [5], it remains an open question whether the optimum can be attained exactly at a finite circuit depth. Likewise, establishing that a transformation is controllable does not quantify the number of unitary evolutions in the basic Hamiltonians required to implement it. In this work, we establish general reachability and circuit synthesis theorems for Hamiltonian variational circuits. When applied to QAOA, these methods guarantee exact finite-depth ground state preparation for a broad class of mixers and yield explicit depth bounds across several standard architectures. The dynamical Lie algebra g associated with a family of control Hamiltonians (see (2)) captures the infinitesimal reachable directions of a quantum circuit. While Lie-algebraic techniques provide foundational controllability criteria in quantum control [9] and have recently proved instrumental in analyzing the expressivity and trainability of variational quantum algorithms [13, 19, 23], standard DLA analysis leaves a gap when applied to state-dependent reachability, as it typically abstracts away both the fixed initial state and the explicit circuit-depth bounds required to synthesize operations from a finite native gate set. Specifically, the minimal g-invariant subspace containing the initial state \(|\xi\rangle\) defines a subspace whose unit sphere contains all states generated by the action of parameterized VQA circuits on \(|\xi\rangle\). However, because circuits implement unitary operations, the true reachable set is the dynamical Lie group _G_ (see (1)) orbit of \(|\xi\rangle\), which forms a ∗ tsvelibor@gmail.com

<tbc>submanifold of that unit sphere of oftentimes significantly lower dimension. Moreover, mere membership in the orbit’s closure does not automatically guarantee attainability via a finite sequence of gate applications without explicit circuit-depth bounds. Finally, knowledge of the generated Lie algebra alone does not specify the required resource overhead, as different generator sets can yield identical algebras at drastically different synthesis costs. This paper’s main goal is to bridge the algebraic, geometric, and circuit-level descriptions.

Let _H_<sub>1</sub>_,...,H<sub>s</sub>_ be a collection of Hamiltonians on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space _W_ and \(|\xi\rangle\) the initial state. We write<tbc>

\(G:=\left\langle e^{-itH_j}|t\in\mathbb{R},1\le j\le s\right\rangle\subseteq U(W)\) (1)

<tbc>for the group of finite native-control products. It is a connected subgroup with dynamical Lie algebra

\(\mathfrak{g}=\langle iH_1,\dots,iH_k\rangle_\mathrm{Lie}\) (2)

and need not be closed in _U(W_).

The elements of _G_ are the unitary transformations that can be implemented exactly by finite sequences of native-control evolutions. In particular, the corresponding variational quantum ansatz generates unitaries of the form

\(U_L(\theta)=e^{-i\theta_LH_{j_L}}\cdots e^{-i\theta_1H_{j_1}},j_\ell\in\{1,\dots,k\}.\) (3)

Here, the sequence **_j_**=(_j_<sub>1</sub>_,...,j<sub>L</sub>_) determines the Hamiltonians applied across successive layers, while \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_L)\in\mathbb{R}^L\) provides the corresponding continuous variational parameters, with _L_ denoting the circuit depth.

Consider an initial state \(|\xi\rangle\). Its projective orbit \(G\cdot[\xi]\) consists of the states attainable (up to a global phase) from \(|\xi\rangle\) by finite circuits as in (3), whereas the closure of this orbit describes asymptotic reachability.

We first establish general criteria for converting asymptotic state preparation into exact, finite-depth realization using parameterized circuits of the form (3) (Section IV). We prove that this exactness property is guaranteed whenever the projective dynamical group, defined as the image of _G_ under the quotient map \(U(W)\rightarrow PU(W)\), is closed, as well as when the initial state is a nondegenerate eigenstate of a generator, even when the group itself is not closed (Theorem IV.4). A related result shows that if an observable _H<sub>P</sub>_ satisfies \(iH_P\in\mathfrak{g}\), its energy infimum over a reachable state orbit is attained by a finite circuit (Theorem IV.8). These statements apply to finite-dimensional Hamiltonian variational ansätze generally; neither full unitary controllability nor a specific layer structure is required.

For QAOA, the exact-reachability criterion yields a broad consequence. If the problem Hamiltonian is diagonal and the mixer is irreducible and stoquastic in the computational basis, the mixer possesses a unique Perron–Frobenius ground state. Prior work demonstrates that QAOA initialized in this state approaches the optimal problem Hamiltonian eigenspace (ground space) asymptotically as the depth increases \[5\]. Our criterion upgrades this conclusion: some _finite_ alternating circuit, utilizing only the original mixer and problem Hamiltonian, prepares an exact ground state (Theorem IV.9). This is a statement regarding attainability; it does not bound the minimum circuit depth nor provide an efficient method for computing the optimal angles.

Exact reachability leaves open the quantitative question of the circuit depth required to attain it. Building on conjugation-based iterative DLA basis construction proposed in \[9\], we derive exact local synthesis depth bounds from the commutator order filtration of the DLA (Theorem VI.4). Importantly, the filtration is constructed directly from the set of generators **a** rather than the DLA g itself. If _c<sub>q</sub>_ new linearly independent Lie algebra directions emerge at filtration level _q_, and D**<sub>a</sub>** is the stabilization depth of the filtration, defined as the minimal index at which the filtration stabilizes (see Definition VI.2), any element within a sufficiently small open neighborhood of the identity in the dynamical Lie group can be synthesized using at most

\(\mathcal{T}_\mathrm{loc}\le\sum_{j=1}^{\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}}(2j-1)c_j\le(2\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}-1)\mathrm{dim}(\mathfrak{g})\) (4)

parametrized exponentials of the basic control Hamiltonians. The corresponding infinitesimal state orbit preparation uses the directions tangent to the orbit, which can be far fewer than the dimension of the group because the state may possess a large _stabilizer_ (i.e., the subgroup of unitaries leaving the state invariant up to a global phase). Thus, the filtration measures how rapidly the physical controls acquire new directions,

<tbc>whereas the orbit determines how many of those directions matter for a particular initial state. The resulting formulas translate abstract Lie-algebraic structure into quantitative _local_ circuit-depth guarantees.

In Section VII we evaluate these bounds across several concrete architectures. Leveraging the general classification framework of \[32\] and the explicit characterization of free Maximum Cut (MaxCut) dynamical Lie algebras \[17, Theorem 1\], we establish system-size-linear stabilization depth bounds for multi-angle QAOA applied to MaxCut on paths, cycles, and complete graphs, accompanied by explicit analytical bounds on circuit depth for local element synthesis. We proceed by establishing the corresponding bounds for reduced MaxCut, Maximum Independent Set (MIS), and Grover-mixer QAOA circuits, whose dynamical Lie algebras have been classified in \[29-31\].

As local charts fail to yield uniform depth bounds across an entire group manifold or orbit, we develop a complementary _global_ synthesis framework for invariant subspaces \(V\subseteq W\) of the ambient Hilbert space on which the DLA restricts to the full or special unitary Lie algebra, u(_V_) or su(_V_) (Theorem VIII.2). While the implications of these algebras for controllability are standard \[10\], the quantitative challenge lies in implementing the required elementary operations using the native control evolutions. To address this, we first establish depth bounds for synthesizing diagonal operations and elementary two-level rotations, and subsequently assemble them via the unitary decomposition techniques of \[27\]. This yields explicit analytic depth bounds for both arbitrary group elements and state-to-state transitions within the sector and its projectivization. Notably, preparing an arbitrary target quantum state can require substantially fewer control steps than implementing an arbitrary unitary operator over the same subspace.

Alternatively, a second global synthesis strategy applies when a fully controllable sector of dimension _D_=2_<sup>q</sup>_ encodes _q_ logical qubits and the restricted DLA is isomorphic to u(_D_) or su(_D_). By combining the quantum Shannon decomposition with the state-preparation framework of \[26\], we express the circuit depth bounds directly in terms of the primitive native implementation costs for single-qubit gates (_K_<sub>1q</sub>) and CNOT gates (_K_<sub>CX</sub>). This yields asymptotic projective unitary-synthesis and state-to-state transfer complexities of \(\mathcal{O}\left(D^2(K_{1\mathrm{q}}+K_\mathrm{CX})\right)\) and O(_D(K_<sub>1q</sub>+_K_<sub>CX</sub>)), respectively (see Theorem VIII.4).

Specifically, our linear stabilization depth estimate for reduced free MaxCut on complete graphs (Theorem VII.5) yields explicit global bounds over its 2<sup>_n_-1</sup>-dimensional reduced Hilbert space (Corollary VIII.6). More broadly, as highlighted in Remark VIII.7, symmetry-reduced ma-QAOA MaxCut instances on graphs, whose reduction is connected and neither bipartite nor cyclic, generate a simple DLA isomorphic to su(2<sup>_n_-1</sup>) on the (_n_-1)-qubit reduced space \[29, Theorem IV.14\]. Consequently, Theorem VIII.5 provides a direct route to global synthesis for these reduced architectures once the generator stabilization depth D<sub>**a**</sub> is determined.

For Maximum Independent Set circuits, whose generators comprise the local _Flip-or-Stay_ mixers introduced in \[30\] alongside individual vertex controls _Z<sub>v</sub>_, the DLA realizes the full unitary algebra on the feasible sector, as established in \[30\]. Letting _D_ denote the number of feasible configurations and \(\Delta_\Gamma\) the diameter of the associated toggle-group Cayley graph, our construction yields explicit circuit-depth bounds of \(\mathcal{O}(D^3\Delta_\Gamma)\) for synthesizing arbitrary unitaries and \(\mathcal{O}(D^2\Delta_\Gamma)\) for arbitrary state-to-state transfers (Theorem VIII.8). This concrete application exemplifies our broader methodological transition: moving past qualitative reachability criteria to rigorously bound the physical resources required to execute quantum operations across the reachable manifold.

Local synthesis bridges reachable-state geometry and variational optimization. Specifically, when the dynamical Lie group _G_ is closed, the problem generator satisfies \(iH_P\in\mathfrak{g}\), and an exact ground state of _H<sub>P</sub>_ is reachable within the orbit, the resulting energy landscape is free of suboptimal local minima. More concretely, from any suboptimal circuit output, one can append an identity-initialized block of bounded native-control depth that exposes either a nonzero energy gradient or a negative-curvature direction (Theorem IX.1). This statement complements QAOA layer-extension results \[24\] and applies to the broader Hamiltonian-control setting under its hypotheses, guaranteeing the existence of a descent direction.

## II. REACHABILITY CONSTRAINTS, LEVEL I (ALGEBRA): CYCLIC REPRESENTATION OF THE DLA GENERATED BY THE INITIAL STATE

To analyze state space reachability in variational quantum ansätze, we first identify the portion of Hilbert space accessible from a given initial state. Such an ansatz generates unitaries of the form

\(U_L(\theta)=\prod_{j=1}^Le^{-i\theta_jA_j},\text{with}A_j\in\{H_1,\dots,H_k\},\) (5)

where \(L\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) denotes the total number of gate applications, \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_L)\in\mathbb{R}^L\) is the vector of real variational parameters, and {_H_<sub>1</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_} is the set of Hermitian operators on the _n_-qubit Hilbert space \(W\cong\mathbb{C}^{2^n}\) corresponding to the circuit’s gate generators (or driving Hamiltonians).

We begin by defining the _dynamical Lie algebra_ associated with the above ansatz as the real Lie algebra generated by the nested commutators of the skew-Hermitian operators {_iH_<sub>1</sub>_,...,iH<sub>k</sub>_}:

\(\mathfrak{g}:=\langle iH_1,\dots,iH_k\rangle_\text{Lie}\subseteq\mathfrak{u}(W).\) (6)

The algebra g governs the complete set of unitary operations accessible to the ansatz and plays a central role in characterizing its control-theoretic properties.

**Remark II.1.** It is important to emphasize that the correspondence between a parameterized quantum circuit architecture and its underlying dynamical Lie algebra is far from unique. Entirely distinct physical generator pools can give rise to the exact same DLA g. This occurs because the DLA is determined solely by the full algebraic closure under the Lie bracket; consequently, different sets of generating operators can share the same DLA.

The following representation-theoretic framework is essential for characterizing the state space limitations of the ansatz.

**Definition II.2.** Let _V_ be a representation space of a Lie algebra g and let \(|\xi\rangle\in V\) be a vector. The _cyclic subrepresentation_ \(V_{\mathfrak{g},|\xi\rangle}\) generated by \(|\xi\rangle\) is the minimal complex g-invariant subspace of _V_ containing \(|\xi\rangle\).

**Remark II.3.** The cyclic subrepresentations considered above share conceptual roots with _Krylov subspaces_, which are ubiquitous in control theory and numerical linear algebra (see, e.g., \[6\]). While a standard Krylov subspace is generated by the successive powers of a single operator _A_ acting on a reference state \(|\xi\rangle\) (i.e., \(\text{span}\{A^k|\xi\rangle\}_{k\ge 0}\), corresponding to the polynomial algebra C\[_A_\]), our cyclic subrepresentation arises from the joint action of a multi-generator Lie algebra g (or equivalently, its universal enveloping algebra) on the state space.

**Remark II.4.** The physical motivation for restricting our analysis to these invariant subspaces stems from the structural constraints of parameterized quantum circuits. As the algorithm is initialized in a reference state \(|\xi\rangle\), the DLA generators preserve the corresponding cyclic subrepresentation of g by definition. Furthermore, since the circuit unitaries are analytic expressions in the generators of g via the group exponential map, the entire state trajectory remains strictly confined within this invariant subspace throughout the unitary evolution prior to final measurement.

In other words, this subspace delineates the dynamically accessible sector of the full Hilbert space. Computing its dimension establishes a fundamental upper bound on the effective variational degrees of freedom that govern the algorithm’s expressiveness--a quantity that is frequently substantially (and in some cases, exponentially) smaller than the ambient dimension 2_<sup>n</sup>_.

## III. REACHABILITY CONSTRAINTS, LEVEL II (GEOMETRY): DYNAMICAL GROUP ORBIT OF THE INITIAL STATE

A common paradigm in assessing the expressibility of a parameterized quantum circuit ansatz relies on analyzing its associated dynamical Lie algebra g (see (6)) and examining the corresponding cyclic subspace \(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi}\) (see Definition II.2). However, the true set of reachable states is in general confined to a lower- dimensional manifold.

<tbc>Specifically, let _G_ denote the connected analytic Lie subgroup of U(_W_) generated by the control Hamiltonians,

\(G:=\langle e^{tA}|A\in\{iH_1,\dots,iH_k\},t\in\mathbb{R}\rangle\subseteq\mathrm{U}(W).\) (7)

By construction, every parameterized VQA unitary \(U_L(\unknown)\) (see (5)) is an element of _G_. Thus, the true reachable set of the parameterized quantum circuits initialized in a unit norm state \(|\xi\rangle\) is given precisely by the dynamical Lie group orbit of the initial state:

\(\mathcal{O}_\xi:=G\cdot|\xi\rangle=\{U|\xi\rangle|U\in G\}\subseteq\mathbb{S}(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi}),\) (8)

where \(\mathbb{S}(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi}):=\{|\psi\rangle\in W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi}|\||\psi\rangle\|=1\}\) denotes the unit sphere of the cyclic subspace \(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi}\). The containment \(\mathcal{O}_\xi\subseteq\mathbb{S}(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi})\) is detailed in Remark II.4.

Next, we establish precise criteria for when the group orbit achieves _maximal reachability_ within the cyclic subspace (modulo global phase)--that is, when the projective orbit of the ray \([\xi]\) generated by \(|\xi\rangle\) completely saturates the projective space:

\(\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}:=G\cdot[\xi]=\mathbb{P}(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi}),\) (9)

where \(\mathbb{P}(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi}):=\mathbb{S}(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi})/\mathrm{U}(1)\) denotes the space of physical quantum states modulo global phase.

**Remark III.1.** Although the classification of Lie subalgebras yielding transitive actions on complex projective spaces is classical, we invoke it here to isolate the precise algebraic criteria ensuring projective transitivity within our framework. The detailed proof is deferred to Appendix A.

**Theorem III.2.** Let _V_ be a complex Hilbert space of dimension \(d\ge 2\), and let \(\mathfrak{g}\subseteq\mathfrak{u}(V)\) be a Lie subalgebra of skew-Hermitian operators. Let \(G=e^\mathfrak{g}\subseteq\mathrm{U}(V)\) be the connected Lie subgroup generated by g, and fix a normalized state \(|\xi\rangle\in V\) .

The projective orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}\) equals the full projective space P(_V_) if and only if, up to a unitary change of basis on _V_ , g is one of the following Lie subalgebras of u(_d_):

1. _full unitary or special unitary algebra:_ su(_d_) or u(_d_) for any \(d\ge 2\).<tbc>

2. _symplectic algebra (or its_ u(1)_-central extension):_ sp(_m_) or \(\mathfrak{sp}(m)\oplus\mathfrak{u}(1)\) when \(d=2m\ge 4\).

For _d_=2, \(\mathfrak{sp}(1)\cong\mathfrak{su}(2)\), which coincides with case (1).

## IV. PERFORMANCE GUARANTEES AND LIMITATIONS

A fundamental geometric property of an orbit \(\mathcal{O}_\xi\) (resp. \(\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}\)) is its topological closed--namely, whether the orbit coincides with its closure \(\overline{\mathcal{O}_\xi}\) in the ambient unit sphere \(\mathbb{S}(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi})\) (resp. \(\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}\) coincides with its closure in the ambient projective space \(\mathbb{P}(W_{\mathfrak{g},\xi})\)). Closedness is the exact orbit property that bridges the gap between asymptotic expressibility and exact reachability: it allows us to elevate convergence guarantees in the infinite depth limit (\(L\rightarrow\infty\)) to rigorous existence guarantees for finite depth parametrized circuits.

Below, we outline several practical and efficiently verifiable criteria ensuring the closedness of these dynamical group orbits. Complete proofs are deferred to Appendix A.

**Theorem IV.1.** Let _H_<sub>1</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_ be Hermitian operators on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space _W_. Let \(\mathfrak{g}\subseteq\mathfrak{u}(W)\) denote the dynamical Lie algebra as in (6) and let \(G\subseteq\mathrm{U}(W)\) be the corresponding connected analytic subgroup as in (7).

If each generator is periodic--that is, for every \(j\in\{1,\dots,k\}\) there exists \(\tau_j\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) such that

\(e^{i\tau_jH_j}=I,\) (10)

then _G_ is a closed subgroup of U(_W_). Consequently, for any normalized state \(|\xi\rangle\in W\), the orbit \(\mathcal{O}_\xi\) is closed in S(_W_).

This periodicity framework applies directly to standard quantum approximate optimization algorithm and VQA ansätze featuring integer or rationally commensurate Hamiltonian spectra.

<tbc>**Example IV.2.** Let _H<sub>M</sub>_ and _H<sub>P</sub>_ be the transverse-field driver and Ising target Hamiltonians on _n_ qubits, defined respectively by<tbc>

\(H_M=\sum_{v=1}^nX_v\text{and}H_P=\sum_{v=1}^nh_vZ_v+\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}J_{uv}Z_uZ_v.\)

<tbc>Suppose that the parameters are rationally commensurate, i.e. there exists \(q\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) such that

\(h_v\in q\mathbb{Z}\text{and}J_{uv}\in q\mathbb{Z}\text{for all}v\in\{1,\dots,n\}\text{and}\{u,v\}\in E.\)

Then _H<sub>M</sub>_ and _H<sub>P</sub>_ are strictly periodic: _H<sub>M</sub>_ has integer spectrum, yielding \(e^{i2\pi H_M}=I\) with period \(\tau_M=2\pi\), while the commuting diagonal terms of _H<sub>P</sub>_ restrict its spectrum to _q_Z, yielding \(e^{i(2\pi/q)H_P}=I\) with period \(\tau_P=2\pi/q\).

By Theorem IV.1, the connected analytic subgroup of \(\mathrm{U}((\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n})\) generated by \(\{e^{itH_M},e^{itH_P}|t\in\mathbb{R}\}\) is closed, and so is the orbit \(\mathcal{O}_\xi\subseteq\mathbb{S}((\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n})\) of any initial state \(\xi\).

**Remark IV.3.** For state-preparation questions, the assumption in (10) can be weakened to projective periodicity. Namely, suppose that, for every _j_, there exist \(\tau_j\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) and \(\theta_j\in\mathbb{R}\) such that

\(e^{i\tau_jH_j}=e^{i\theta_j}I.\) (11)

Applying Theorem IV.1 to the images of the generators in the projective unitary group \(\mathrm{PU}(W)\cong\mathrm{U}(W)/\mathrm{U}(1)\) shows that the projective image of _G_ is closed. Consequently, every projective _G_-orbit in P(_W_) is closed.

## A. Orbit Closedness and Finite Depth Guarantees

While expressiveness analyses often characterize the states reachable in the asymptotic limit of infinite depth, physical VQA implementations require exact state preparation using finite-depth architectures. The topological closedness of the dynamical Lie group orbit plays a pivotal role here, establishing a direct equivalence between infinite-depth asymptotic limits and exact finite-depth expressiveness.

The primary practical significance of orbit closedness is illustrated in Figure 2. Specifically, any projectivized target state \[_t_\] obtained as a limit of state sequences produced by parameterized quantum circuits of the form (5) as the circuit depth \(L\rightarrow\infty\) lies by definition in the topological closure \(\overline{\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}}\) of the dynamical Lie group orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}=G\cdot[\xi]\).

When the orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}\) is closed--as guaranteed, for instance, when _G_ is compact under the periodic conditions of Theorem IV.1 (or Remark IV.3), the orbit coincides with its closure \((\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}=\overline{\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}})\). Consequently, any state \(|t\rangle\) reachable in the infinite-depth limit can in fact be represented _exactly_ as \(|t\rangle=e^{i\phi} g|\xi\rangle\) for some \(g\in G\) and \(\phi\in[0,2\pi]\). In turn, because _G_ is the connected Lie group generated by the skew-Hermitian operators \(\{iH_j\}_{j=1}^k\), every \(g\in G\) admits an exact synthesis as a finite-depth parameterized circuit of the form (5). Thus, orbit closedness closes the gap between asymptotic and exact expressiveness, ensuring that no target state requires infinite depth to be realized.

We establish the following general reachability criteria.

**Theorem IV.4.** Let _H_<sub>1</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_ be a collection of Hamiltonians on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space _W_, let \(\mathfrak{g}\subseteq\mathfrak{u}(W)\) denote the corresponding dynamical Lie algebra (see (6)), and let \(G\subseteq\mathrm{U}(W)\) be the corresponding connected analytic subgroup.

Suppose that \(|s\rangle,|t\rangle\in W\) are nonzero vectors satisfying<tbc>

\([t]\in\overline{\mathcal{O}_{[s]}}.\) (12)

<tbc>Let

\(\pi:\mathrm{U}(W)\longrightarrow\mathrm{PU}(W)\)

denote the canonical projective quotient map.

Assume, in addition, that at least one of the following conditions holds:

1. The projective subgroup \(\pi(G)\subseteq\mathrm{PU}(W)\) is closed. This holds, in particular, under the periodicity conditions of (11).<tbc>

2. The vector \(|s\rangle\) is an eigenvector of some _H<sub>r</sub>_, \(1\le r\le k\), and its corresponding eigenspace is one- dimensional.

Then there exist an integer \(L\ge 0\), indices<tbc>

\(j_1,\dots,j_L\in\{1,\dots,k\},\)

<tbc>and collection of parameters \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_L)\in\mathbb{R}^L\) such that

\(U_L(\theta)\cdot[s]=[t]\) (13)

with \(U_L(\theta)\) as in (5).

**Remark IV.5.** Every product ansatz of the form (5) in Theorem IV.4 can also be expressed using the fixed-order layered ansatz

\(U_L(\theta)=\prod_{\ell=1}^L\left(e^{-i\theta_{\ell,k}H_k}\cdots e^{-i\theta_{\ell,1}H_1}\right),\) (14)

where the product is time-ordered from right to left. Indeed, one may use a single nonzero parameter in each layer \(\ell\) corresponding to generator \(H_{j_\ell}\), setting all remaining parameters within that layer equal to zero.

For _k_=2, with _H_<sub>1</sub>=_H<sub>P</sub>_ and _H_<sub>2</sub>=_H<sub>M</sub>_, equation (14) reduces to the standard QAOA circuit

\(U_p(\beta,\gamma)=\prod_{k=1}^pe^{-i\beta_kH_M}e^{-i\gamma_kH_P}=e^{-i\beta_pH_M}e^{-i\gamma_pH_P}\cdots e^{-i\beta_1H_M}e^{-i\gamma_1H_P},\) (15)

where \(\beta=(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p)\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(\gamma=(\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_p)\in\mathbb{R}^p\) are variational parameters.

**Corollary IV.6.** Suppose that the DLA g admits a decomposition

\(\mathfrak{g}=[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}]\oplus\mathfrak{c},\mathfrak{c}\subseteq i\mathbb{R}I_W.\) (16)

Then every projective _G_-orbit is closed. Consequently, for any non-zero states \(|s\rangle,|t\rangle\in W\),

\([t]\in\overline{G\cdot[s]}\)

implies that \(|t\rangle\) is exactly (up to a global phase) reachable from \(|s\rangle\) by a finite parameterized circuit.

In particular, the conclusion holds whenever g is semisimple.

<tbc>**Example IV.7.** The preceding corollary applies to several classes of dynamical Lie algebras arising in quantum optimization.

First, consider the free (multi-angle) MaxCut QAOA ansatz defined on a connected graph \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) with \(n:=|V|\ge 2\). Its dynamical Lie algebra is given by

\(\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{free}}=\langle iX_v,iZ_uZ_v|v\in V,(u,v)\in E\rangle_\mathrm{Lie}.\) (17)

By the structural classification in \[17, Theorem 1\], \(\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{free}}\) belongs to one of six families, each of which is either a compact simple Lie algebra or a direct sum of compact simple Lie algebras. Consequently, \(\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{free}}\) is semisimple, which implies that the corresponding dynamical Lie group is closed \[18, Proposition 7.9\]. Thus, Theorem IV.4 implies that whenever a target ray belongs to the closure of the orbit of the initial one, it is exactly reachable by a finite multi-angle circuit.

This conclusion extends directly to general (not necessarily connected) graphs. If a graph has no isolated vertices, its free DLA decomposes into a direct sum of the DLAs associated with its connected components, thereby satisfying the hypotheses of Corollary IV.6 with c=0.

More generally, let A={_iP_<sub>1</sub>_,...,iP<sub>m</sub>_} be a Lie-algebraically independent set of skew-Hermitian Pauli strings, and let C(A) be its anticommutation graph, whose vertices represent the generators _iP<sub>j</sub>_ and whose edges join pairs \((iP_j,iP_\ell)\) that anticommute \((P_jP_\ell=-P_\ell P_j)\). Suppose that C(A) is connected and contains at least two vertices.

According to the classification of Pauli-generated Lie algebras in \[1, Theorem 2\], the generated Lie algebra

\(\mathfrak{g}_\mathcal{A}:=\langle iP_1,\dots,iP_m\rangle_\mathrm{Lie}\) (18)

is isomorphic to a direct sum of classical compact simple Lie algebras of type so(_d_), sp(_d_), or su(_d_), where the specific algebra and rank are uniquely determined by the topology of C(A) and the algebraic relations among its generators. Thus, g<sub>A</sub> is semisimple, every projective orbit generated by the corresponding circuit architecture is closed, and exact finite reachability holds due to Theorem IV.4 .

**Theorem IV.8.** Let _H_<sub>1</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_ be a collection of Hamiltonians on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space _W_, let \(\mathfrak{g}\subseteq\mathfrak{u}(W)\) denote the corresponding dynamical Lie algebra (see (6)), and let \(G\subseteq\mathrm{U}(W)\) be the corresponding connected Lie subgroup. Suppose that the target observable _H<sub>P</sub>_ satisfies<tbc>

\(iH_P\in\mathfrak{g}.\)

<tbc>Then, for any initial state \(|s\rangle\) with density matrix \(\rho_s:=|s\rangle\langle s|\), the infimum of the expectation value of _H<sub>P</sub>_ over the reachable state manifold,

\(\mathrm{inf}_{g\in G}\mathrm{Tr}\left(H_Pg\rho_sg^\dagger\right)\)

is attained by a finite parametrized circuit of the form given in (5) in the original controls. In particular, if the infimum coincides with the global ground state energy of _H<sub>P</sub>_, an exact ground state can be reached by a finite-depth circuit within the ansatz.

## B. Finite-Depth Ground Space Reachability Guarantees in QAOA

While general state controllability concerns the reachability of arbitrary pure states, in many practical applications, particularly classical combinatorial optimization, our primary interest lies in the reachability of the optimal solution subspace rather than a specific target state.

Let \(W=(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}\) denote the _n_-qubit Hilbert space equipped with the computational basis \(\{|s\rangle\}_{s\in\{0,1\}^n}\). Let _H<sub>P</sub>_ be the problem Hamiltonian acting on _W_, which encodes a classical objective function<tbc>

\(F:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\)

<tbc>via \(H_P|s\rangle=F(s)|s\rangle\). Let \(\lambda_\mathrm{min}:=\mathrm{min}_{s\in\{0,1\}^n}F(s)\) denote the ground state energy of _H<sub>P</sub>_, and let \(H_{P,\mathrm{min}}\subseteq W\) denote its corresponding ground space:

\(H_{P,\mathrm{min}}:=\mathrm{span}\left\{|s\rangle|s\in\{0,1\}^n,F(s)=\lambda_\mathrm{min}\right\}.\) (19)

<tbc>Suppose that the mixer Hamiltonian _H<sub>M</sub>_ in QAOA is _stoquastic_ with respect to the computational basis, meaning its off-diagonal elements satisfy \(\langle s|H_M|t\rangle\le 0\) for all distinct \(s,t\in\{0,1\}^n\), and _irreducible_, in the sense that it has no stable proper coordinate subspaces.

By the Perron-Frobenius theorem, the ground state space of _H<sub>M</sub>_ is one-dimensional. Let \(|\xi\rangle\) denote a unit vector spanning this space.

Given _H<sub>M</sub>_ as above and _H<sub>P</sub>_ diagonal in the computational basis, it was shown in \[5\] that the QAOA ansatz, initialized at \(|\xi\rangle\), asymptotically prepares a state within the minimum-energy sector _H_<sub>_P,_min</sub> as the circuit depth \(p\rightarrow\infty\).

Since every parametrized quantum circuit representing the QAOA ansatz (see (15)) is structurally confined to the dynamical Lie group _G_, satisfying the Perron-Frobenius conditions imposes the non-trivial overlap constraint on the initial state orbit closure:

\(\overline{G\cdot[\xi]}\cap\mathbb{P}(H_{P,\mathrm{min}})\neq\varnothing.\) (20)

The following result is a particular instance of Theorem IV.4 (by setting _H<sub>r</sub>=H<sub>M</sub>_). It demonstrates that under mild conditions on the mixer, the orbit of the initial state is closed, thereby upgrading the standard infinite-depth asymptotic convergence of QAOA to an exact, finite-depth reachability guarantee.

**Theorem IV.9.** Let _W_ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space equipped with a computational basis. Let \(H_P,H_M\in\mathrm{Herm}(W)\) be Hermitian operators such that _H<sub>P</sub>_ is diagonal in the computational basis, and _H<sub>M</sub>_ is irreducible and stoquastic in the same basis. Let \(|\xi\rangle\) be the unique normalized ground state of _H<sub>M</sub>_ .

Then, there exist a finite circuit depth \(L\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), parameter vectors \(\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^L\), a normalized ground state \(|\zeta\rangle\in H_{P,\mathrm{min}}\), and a global phase \(\phi\in\mathbb{R}\) such that

\(U_L(\beta,\gamma)|\xi\rangle=|\zeta\rangle,\) (21)

where \(U_L(\beta,\gamma)\) is defined as in (15).

Consequently, the infinite-depth asymptotic convergence guarantee of QAOA is promoted to an exact finite-depth reachability guarantee.

**Remark IV.10.** While Theorem IV.9 establishes a qualitative existence guarantee, it is non-constructive in nature, as it neither provides explicit target-specific depth bounds nor yields concrete parameter optimization procedures.

## V. GEOMETRY VS ALGEBRA: SMALL ORBITS WITH EXPONENTIALLY MANY LINEARLY INDEPENDENT OPTIMA

A fundamental geometric feature of the dynamical Lie group orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\xi]}\subseteq\mathbb{P}(W)\) generated by the ray of an initial state \(|\xi\rangle\) is that it forms a smooth, connected manifold rather than a linear subspace. Consequently, a low-dimensional orbit can _curve_ through projective Hilbert space in such a way that the states inside it span a high-dimensional vector subspace.

In this section, we present an explicit example of this phenomenon, arising from a fixed-particle _XY_ ansatz, where the orbit of quadratic dimension O(_n_<sup>2</sup>) in the number of qubits _n_ contains exponentially many linearly independent ground states of the problem Hamiltonian _H<sub>P</sub>_. Although the underlying classical optimization task in this construction is intentionally simple, its primary purpose is to vividly demonstrate that low orbit dimensionality poses no intrinsic barrier to capturing exponentially many solutions or achieving exact ground space reachability in variational quantum algorithms.

Let \(n\ge 2\), \(1\le k\le n-1\), and consider the fixed-excitation (fixed-Hamming-weight) subspace<tbc>

\(W_k:=\mathrm{span}\left\{|S\rangle|S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\},|S|=k\right\}.\) (22)

<tbc>Here, _S_ records the occupied qubit sites, and \(N_j:=\frac{I-Z_j}{2}=|1\rangle\langle 1|_j\) is the occupation-number operator at site _j_. We consider the nearest-neighbor _XY_ path mixer _H<sub>M</sub>_ paired with an endpoint problem Hamiltonian _H<sub>P</sub>_:

\(H_M:=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\left(X_jX_{j+1}+Y_jY_{j+1}\right),H_P:=N_1.\) (23)

<tbc>**Remark V.1.** Physically, _H<sub>M</sub>_ corresponds to the isotropic limit (\(\gamma=0\)) of the 1D _XY_ spin chain with free boundary conditions introduced by Lieb, Schultz, and Mattis \[20\]. The problem Hamiltonian _H<sub>P</sub>=N_<sub>1</sub> acts as a localized boundary potential (or single-site occupation pin). Particle-number-preserving _XY_ mixers of this form serve as a standard mechanism for hard-constrained optimization in the Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz \[16\].

The mixer _H<sub>M</sub>_ in (23) generates nearest-neighbor excitation-hopping transitions, thereby commuting with the total particle-number operator \(\sum_{j=1}^nN_j\) and preserving each fixed-particle subspace _W<sub>k</sub>_ defined in (22). When restricted to _W<sub>k</sub>_, the operator _H<sub>M</sub>_|<sub>_W<sub>k</sub>_</sub> is irreducible with entrywise non-positive off-diagonal matrix elements in the computational basis. Consequently, by the Perron-Frobenius theorem, _H<sub>M</sub>_|<sub>_W<sub>k</sub>_</sub> possesses a unique ground state \(|\xi_k\rangle\), whose computational basis expansion coefficients are strictly positive. Furthermore, the optimal configurations for the problem Hamiltonian _H<sub>P</sub>=N_<sub>1</sub> within _W<sub>k</sub>_ are precisely those computational basis states \(|S\rangle\) for which site 1 is unoccupied (\(1\notin S\)):

\(W_{P,\mathrm{min}}=\mathrm{ker}\big(N_1\big|_{W_k}\big)=\mathrm{span}\{|S\rangle|S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\},|S|=k,1\notin S\}\) (24)

and has real dimension

\(\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}(W_{P,\mathrm{min}})=2\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-1}{k}.\) (25)

The following proposition establishes that the initial state \(|\xi_k\rangle\) generates a low-dimensional orbit that nonetheless spans the entire subspace _W<sub>k</sub>_ and contains exponentially many exact optima.

**Proposition V.2.** Let \(W_k\subset(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}\) be the _k_-Hamming weight subspace defined in (22), let

\(\mathfrak{g}_{n,k}=\left\langle iH_M\big|_{W_k},iH_P\big|_{W_k}\right\rangle_\mathrm{Lie}\)

be the associated dynamical Lie algebra, and let \(G_{n,k}\subseteq\mathrm{U}(W_k)\) be its connected dynamical Lie group. Then, for an initial reference state \(|\xi_k\rangle\) corresponding to a single Slater determinant formed by _k_ occupied single-particle orbitals, the DLA g_<sub>n,k</sub>_, the projective orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\xi_k]}=G_{n,k}\cdot[\xi_k]\), and the cyclic subrepresentation \(W_{\mathfrak{g}_{n,k},|\xi_k\rangle}\) satisfy:

\(\mathfrak{g}_{n,k}\cong\mathfrak{u}(n),\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}(\mathfrak{g}_{n,k})=n^2,\) (26)

\(\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}\mathcal{O}_{[\xi_k]}=2k(n-k),\) (27)

\(W_{\mathfrak{g}_{n,k},|\xi_k\rangle}=W_k,\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}(W_{\mathfrak{g}_{n,k},|\xi_k\rangle})=2\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k}.\) (28)

All \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-1}{k}\) optimal computational basis states are exactly reachable, up to a global phase, by finite alternating circuits as in (15).

**Remark V.3.** At half-filling \(k=\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\), both the cyclic space dimension and the number of mutually orthogonal reachable optimal states grow exponentially as \(n\rightarrow\infty\):

\(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k}=\Theta\left(\frac{2^n}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\mathrm{and}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-1}{k}=\Theta\left(\frac{2^n}{\sqrt{n}}\right),\) (29)

whereas the dynamical Lie algebra orbit dimension scales only quadratically as O(_n_<sup>2</sup>).

A complete, rigorous proof of Proposition V.2, together with its representation-theoretic details and geometric interpretations, is provided in Appendix B; a schematic overview of this geometric phenomenon is illustrated in Figure 3.

## VI. CIRCUIT DEPTH BOUNDS FOR NEAR-IDENTITY GROUP ELEMENTS AND LOCAL FLOWS ALONG THE STATE ORBIT MANIFOLD

In this section, we analyze the expressibility of parameterized variational quantum algorithm circuits of the form (5) when synthesizing elements within a sufficiently small open neighborhood \(U_I\subseteq G\) of the identity element _I_ in the dynamical Lie group _G_. Our primary objective is to derive an upper bound on the circuit depth _L_, defined as the minimum number of exponential factors in the DLA generators required to generate any element \(g\in U_I\). We first establish a uniform bound for local element synthesis expressed in terms of the _stabilization depth_ of a natural filtration associated with the generators of a dynamical Lie algebra g (see (6)). We then sharpen this bound for local state evolution along the orbit manifold \(\mathcal{O}_{[\psi]}\) of a reference state \(|\psi\rangle\). While points states in an open neighborhood of \([\psi]\) within the orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\psi]}\) can be expressed as \(g\cdot[\psi]\) for \(g\in U_I\), elements of the isotropy subgroup

\(\mathrm{Stab}_G([\psi]):=\{g\in G|g\cdot|\psi\rangle=e^{i\phi}|\psi\rangle\}\)

leave the projective state invariant up to a global phase. By factoring out these redundant stabilizer directions, we obtain a tighter, state-dependent bound on the circuit depth required to generate local flows along the state orbit. We note that the bounds derived in this section are structural existence guarantees for short-depth local control; they do not explicitly yield the optimal parameter values needed to synthesize a target gate or state.

## A. Local Canonical Coordinates and Stabilization Depth

A central tool for establishing the existence of the aforementioned local parametrization, we employ the product-of-exponentials map, defining _canonical coordinates of the second kind_ on the dynamical Lie group, a foundational tool in geometric control theory and variational quantum circuit design.

Given an ordered basis {_b_<sub>1</sub>_,...,b<sub>n</sub>_} of g (where _n_=dimg), this map is defined as

\(\varphi_\mathfrak{g}:\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow G,\varphi_\mathfrak{g}(x):=e^{x_1b_1}\cdots e^{x_nb_n},\) (30)

where \(x=\sum_{i=1}^nx_ib_i\in\mathfrak{g}\).

**Remark VI.1.** The map \(\varphi_\mathfrak{g}\) provides a factorized local parametrization around the identity in terms of a product of one-parameter subgroups, in contrast to the standard exponential map \(x\mapsto e^x\). By construction, \(\varphi_\mathfrak{g}\) maps the origin of the Lie algebra to the group identity, i.e., \(\varphi_\mathfrak{g}(0)=I\).

As a finite product of smooth exponential maps, \(\varphi_\mathfrak{g}\) is smooth. Furthermore, its differential at the origin is the identity transformation, \((d\varphi_\mathfrak{g})_0=\mathrm{id}_\mathfrak{g}\). By the Inverse Function Theorem, there exist open neighborhoods \(V_0\subseteq\mathfrak{g}\) containing 0 and \(U_{I,\varphi_\mathfrak{g}}\subseteq G\) containing _I_ such that

\(\varphi_\mathfrak{g}:V_0-\rightarrow^\cong U_{I,\varphi_\mathfrak{g}}\) (31)

is a smooth local diffeomorphism. Consequently, any element \(g\in U_{I,\varphi_\mathfrak{g}}\) can be uniquely factorized into the product form (30).

Following the framework of \[9, Section 2\], we represent elements of the open neighborhood \(U_{I,\varphi_\mathfrak{g}}\subseteq G\) (see (31)) in the parameterized circuit form as in (5). To analyze and bound the resulting circuit depth _L_, we leverage an ascending vector space filtration that stratifies g according to the minimal bracket depth required to generate its elements from the set of original generators **a**={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>k</sub>_} of g (here we assume that the generators are linearly independent over R).

More precisely, let g be a finite-dimensional (real) Lie algebra presented by a set of generators. It is natural to organize the elements of g according to the minimum bracket depth required to generate them. This induces an ascending vector space filtration on g:

\(\{0\}=\mathcal{F}_0^\mathbf{a}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_1^\mathbf{a}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_2^\mathbf{a}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathfrak{g},\) (32)

defined recursively as follows.

• **Base layer:** the subspace spanned by the generators, \(\mathcal{F}_1^\mathbf{a}:=\mathrm{span}_\mathbb{R}\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}\).<tbc>

• **Higher layers:** \(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a}:=\mathcal{F}_{j-1}^\mathbf{a}+[\mathcal{F}_1^\mathbf{a},\mathcal{F}_{j-1}^\mathbf{a}]\) for \(j\ge 2\), which ensures the bracket compatibility condition

\([\mathcal{F}_{d_1}^\mathbf{a},\mathcal{F}_{d_2}^\mathbf{a}]\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{d_1+d_2}^\mathbf{a}.\) (33)

As g is finite-dimensional, this ascending filtration of subspaces must eventually stabilize at g. This allows us to formalize the notion of _stabilization depth_.

**Definition VI.2.** Let **a**={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>k</sub>_} be a set of generators. The _stabilization depth_ of **a** is the minimal index at which the filtration sequence (32) stabilizes:

\(\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}:=\mathrm{min}\{j\in\mathbb{N}|\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a}=\mathcal{F}_{j+1}^\mathbf{a}\}.\) (34)

Equivalently, D**<sub>a</sub>** is the minimal integer _j_ such that any Lie word of length greater than _j_ lies within the linear span of Lie words of length at most _j_.

To express every element \(g\in U_{I,\varphi_\mathfrak{g}}\subseteq G\) (see (31)) in the circuit form (5), we construct an ordered basis {_b_<sub>1</sub>_,...,b<sub>n</sub>_} of g from nested conjugates of the original generators **a**={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>k</sub>_}. We initialize the construction by setting

\(b_i=a_i,1\le i\le k.\)

<tbc>Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). For each \(j\ge 1\), define the subset<tbc>

\(\mathcal{C}_j(\varepsilon):=\left\{\mathrm{Ad}_{e^{t_1a_i_1\dots e^{t_qa_i_q}}}(a_{i_0})\right|\left|\begin{array}{ c }
0\le q\le j-1, \\
i_0,\dots,i_q\in\{1,\dots,k\}, \\
|t_r|<\varepsilon,1\le r\le q
\end{array}\right\}\subseteq\mathfrak{g},\)

<tbc>where the product is understood as the identity when _q_=0, and consider the subspace

\(S_j(\varepsilon):=\mathrm{span}_\mathbb{R}\mathcal{C}_j(\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathfrak{g}.\)

Thus, \(\mathcal{C}_j(\varepsilon)\) contains conjugates evaluated at all parameter values in the indicated intervals, rather than at a single fixed choice of parameters. In particular, \(S_1(\varepsilon)=\mathcal{F}_1^\mathbf{a}\).

We first show that

\(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a}\subseteq S_j(\varepsilon)(j\ge 1).\) (35)

Indeed, let \(c\in S_{j-1}(\varepsilon)\). Writing _c_ as a finite linear combination of elements of \(\mathcal{C}_{j-1}(\varepsilon)\) and using the linearity of the adjoint action shows that<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Ad}_{e^{ta_i}}(c)\in S_j(\varepsilon)\text{for every}|t|<\varepsilon.\)

<tbc>Since \(c\in S_{j-1}(\varepsilon)\subseteq S_j(\varepsilon)\), we have, for every nonzero \(|t|<\varepsilon\),

\(\frac{\mathrm{Ad}_{e^{ta_i}}(c)-c}{t}\in S_j(\varepsilon).\) (36)

The space \(S_j(\varepsilon)\) is a linear subspace of the finite-dimensional normed space g, and is therefore closed. Taking the limit of (36) as \(t\rightarrow 0\) gives

\([a_i,c]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\mathrm{Ad}_{e^{ta_i}}(c)\in S_j(\varepsilon).\) (37)

The recursive definition of the filtration (see (33)) now proves (35) by induction on _j_.

We next select the basis elements. Suppose that, through stage _j_-1, we have selected exactly \(\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{F}_{j-1}^\mathbf{a})\) linearly independent elements within \(\mathcal{C}_{j-1}(\varepsilon)\), and let _W_<sub>_j_-1</sub> denote their span. Since<tbc>

\(W_{j-1}\subseteq S_{j-1}(\varepsilon)\subseteq S_j(\varepsilon)\)

<tbc>and \(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a}\subseteq S_j(\varepsilon)\), we obtain

\(\mathrm{dim}\big(S_j(\varepsilon)/W_{j-1}\big)=\mathrm{dim}(S_j(\varepsilon))-\mathrm{dim}(W_{j-1})\ge\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a})-\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{F}_{j-1}^\mathbf{a}).\) (38)

As \(\mathcal{C}_j(\varepsilon)\) spans \(S_j(\varepsilon)\), its image spans the quotient \(S_j(\varepsilon)/W_{j-1}\). We may therefore select

\(c_j:=\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a})-\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{F}_{j-1}^\mathbf{a})\)

elements of \(\mathcal{C}_j(\varepsilon)\) whose cosets are linearly independent in \(S_j(\varepsilon)/W_{j-1}\). Appending these elements to the previously selected collection produces a linearly independent set of cardinality \(\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a})\).

Repeating the preceding selection through stage D<sub>**a**</sub> (see Definition VI.2) produces _n_=dim(g) linearly independent elements and hence a basis {_b_<sub>1</sub>_,...,b<sub>n</sub>_} of g.

**Remark VI.3.** The argument of Ref. \[9, Section 2\] also gives a useful criterion for making individual selections. Suppose that _W_ is the span of the elements already selected and that an available conjugate<tbc>

\(c\in W\cap\mathcal{C}_{j-1}(\varepsilon)\)

<tbc>satisfies \([a_i,c]\notin W\). Let \(\pi_W:\mathfrak{g}\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}/W\) denote the quotient map. Since \(c\in W\), the expansion

\(\mathrm{Ad}_{e^{ta_i}}(c)=c+t[a_i,c]+O(t^2)\)

<tbc>gives<tbc>

\(\pi_W(\mathrm{Ad}_{e^{ta_i}}(c))=t\pi_W([a_i,c])+O(t^2).\)

<tbc>Equivalently,<tbc>

\(\frac{1}{t}\pi_W(\mathrm{Ad}_{e^{ta_i}}(c))\longrightarrow\pi_W([a_i,c])\neq 0\text{as}t\rightarrow 0.\)

<tbc>It follows that there exists \(\delta>0\) such that

\(b_m:=\mathrm{Ad}_{e^{ta_i}}(c)\notin W\text{whenever}0<|t|<\mathrm{min}\{\delta,\varepsilon\}.\) (39)

Thus every sufficiently small nonzero conjugation parameter supplies a new linearly independent direction.

The same conjugation structure gives an exact synthesis of every selected flow. Indeed, if _b<sub>m</sub>_ is selected at stage _j_, then \(b_m\in\mathcal{C}_j(\varepsilon)\), so it has the form<tbc>

\(b_m=\mathrm{Ad}_{P_m}(a_{i_0}),P_m=e^{t_1a_{i_1}}\cdots e^{t_qa_{i_q}},q\le j-1.\)

<tbc>Therefore, for every \(s\in\mathbb{R}\),<tbc>

\(e^{sb_m}=e^{sP_ma_{i_0}P_m^{-1}}=P_me^{sa_{i_0}}P_m^{-1}=e^{t_1a_{i_1}}\cdots e^{t_qa_{i_q}}e^{sa_{i_0}}e^{-t_qa_{i_q}}\cdots e^{-t_1a_{i_1}}.\)

<tbc>In particular, if _b<sub>m</sub>_=Ad_<sub>e<sup>ta<sub>i</sub></sup></sub>(c_), then<tbc>

\(e^{sb_m}=e^{ta_i}e^{sc}e^{-ta_i}.\)

<tbc>Although _c_ need not be a selected basis element, its membership in \(\mathcal{C}_{j-1}(\varepsilon)\) supplies an exact native factorization of _e<sup>sc</sup>_. Hence _e<sup>sb<sub>m</sub></sup>_ is synthesized using at most

\(2q+1\le 2(j-1)+1\le 2j-1\)

native generator flows, without Trotterization or Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff approximations.

If _b<sub>m</sub>_ is selected at filtration stage _j_, then \(b_m\in\mathcal{C}_j(\varepsilon)\). Hence, as shown in Remark VI.3, the corresponding flow _e<sup>sb<sub>m</sub></sup>_ admits an exact factorization into at most 2_j_-1 native generator flows. Since precisely<tbc>

\(c_j:=\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a})-\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{F}_{j-1}^\mathbf{a})\)

<tbc>basis elements are selected at stage _j_, concatenating these factorizations in the canonical-coordinate representation \(\varphi_\mathfrak{g}\) shows that every \(g\in U_{I,\varphi_\mathfrak{g}}\) can be represented using at most

\(\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{a}:=\sum_{j=1}^{\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}}(2j-1)c_j\) (40)

native exponential factors. Thus T<sub>**a**</sub> is a uniform upper bound furnished by the construction; cancellations or shorter conjugating words may reduce the number of factors required for a particular group element.

For any non-abelian Lie algebra g, this operation count satisfies the elementary bounds

\(\mathrm{dim}(\mathfrak{g})\le\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{a}<\mathrm{dim}^2(\mathfrak{g}).\) (41)

Since \(j\le\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}\) and \(\sum_jc_j=\mathrm{dim}(\mathfrak{g})\), (40) yields the refined upper bound

\(\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{a}\le(2\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}-1)\mathrm{dim}\mathfrak{g}.\) (42)

These observations establish a stabilization depth dependent bound on local circuit synthesis complexity, summarized in the following theorem.

**Theorem VI.4.** Let \(\mathfrak{g}\subseteq\mathfrak{u}(W)\) be a dynamical Lie algebra generated by {_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>k</sub>_} with stabilization depth D<sub>**a**</sub>. Then every element _g_ in the identity neighborhood \(U_{I,\varphi_\mathfrak{g}}\subseteq G\) (cf. (31)) admits a finite product- of-exponentials decomposition

\(g=e^{\theta_La_{j_L}}\cdots e^{\theta_1a_{j_1}},\) (43)

where \(a_{j_s}\in\{a_1,\dots,a_k\}\) for each \(s\in\{1,\dots,\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{a}\}\), and the required depth \(L\le\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{a}\) satisfies (42). In particular, this bounds the local parameterization depth to O(D<sub>**a**</sub>dimg).

## B. Circuit Depth Bounds for Infinitesimal Evolutions of States

Let \(|\psi\rangle\in W\) be a unit vector (\(\|\psi\|=1\)). The real dimension \(m_\psi\) of the projective _G_-orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\psi]}\) satisfies<tbc>

\(m_\psi:=\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}\big(\mathcal{O}_{[\psi]}\big)=\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}\big(\mathfrak{g}\big)-\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}\big(\mathrm{stab}_\mathfrak{g}([\psi])\big),\) (44)

<tbc>where

\(\mathrm{stab}_\mathfrak{g}([\psi]):=\big\{A\in\mathfrak{g}|A|\psi\rangle\in i\mathbb{R}|\psi\rangle\big\}\) (45)

is the Lie algebra stabilizer of \([\psi]\) in g.

For the DLA filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a}\}_{j\ge 1}\) generated by the original controls **a**={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>k</sub>_} (see (32)), define<tbc>

\(r_j(\psi):=\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}\big\{(I-|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)A|\psi\rangle\big|A\in\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a}\big\},r_0(\psi):=0.\) (46)

<tbc>Thus, \(r_j(\psi)\) counts the number of linearly independent infinitesimal directions in the tangent space of the projective orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\psi]}\) generated by the _j_-th filtered subspace of g. In particular,<tbc>

\(r_j(\psi)=\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a})-\mathrm{dim}_\mathbb{R}(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a}\cap\mathrm{stab}_\mathfrak{g}([\psi])).\) (47)

<tbc>Let

\(\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{a},\psi}:=\mathrm{min}\big\{j\in\mathbb{N}|r_j(\psi)=m_\psi\big\}.\) (48)

be the \(\psi\)_-stabilization depth_ of the generating set **a**, representing the minimal number of filtration steps required to fully span the tangent space of the projective orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\psi]}\).

**Remark VI.5.** It follows from (47) that for all \(j\ge 1\):<tbc>

\(r_j(\psi)\le\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{F}_j^\mathbf{a}),\) (49)

<tbc>which, in turn, implies the state-independent uniform bounds

## VII. STABILIZATION DEPTH BOUNDS FOR QAOA ARCHITECTURES

Next we compute explicit bounds on the stabilization depth D<sub>**a**</sub> for several prominent families of parameterized quantum circuits. Specifically, we analyze the dynamical Lie algebras associated with multi-angle QAOA ansätze applied to various combinatorial optimization problems, as well as Grover-mixer QAOA (GM-QAOA) architectures. These concrete bounds characterize the bracket depth required to exhaust the underlying Lie algebra, thereby yielding explicit upper bounds on the local circuit depth required for expressivity near the identity of the group.

In Subsection VIIE, we leverage these results to establish explicit circuit-depth upper bounds for local unitary synthesis and state preparation. A rigorous treatment and full technical proofs for these stabilization depth derivations are provided in Appendix C.

**Remark VII.1.** The stabilization depth D<sub>**a**</sub> is defined relative to a specific choice of generating set \(\mathbf{a}\subset\mathfrak{g}\) rather than the Lie algebra g itself (see Definition VI.2). However, each circuit architecture considered in this section is equipped with a canonical, predefined set of elementary gate generators (e.g., individual Pauli terms or driver/problem Hamiltonian components). Consequently, when the generating set **a** is unambiguous from context, we adopt the slight abuse of notation \(\mathcal{D}_\mathfrak{g}\equiv\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}\) to denote the stabilization depth of the corresponding dynamical Lie algebra.

### A. Dynamical Lie Algebras for the MaxCut Problem QAOA

The Maximum Cut problem on a finite graph \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) seeks a vertex partition maximizing the number of crossing edges. In the standard Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm framework, this combinatorial problem is mapped to an Ising spin system defined by the transverse-field mixer _B_ and problem Hamiltonian _H<sub>P</sub>_:

\(B=\sum_{w\in V}X_w,H_P=\sum_{\{v,w\}\in E}Z_vZ_w.\) (54)

The associated standard dynamical Lie algebra is generated by these two collective operators:

\(\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{std}}:=\left\langle iB,iH_P\right\rangle_\mathrm{Lie}.\) (55)

In multi-angle QAOA, each individual term in the mixer and problem Hamiltonians is assigned an independent variational parameter. The corresponding _free_ dynamical Lie algebra is formed by taking these individual operators as separate control fields:

\(\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{free}}:=\left\langle\{iX_w|w\in V\}\cup\{iZ_vZ_w|\{v,w\}\in E\}\right\rangle_\mathrm{Lie}.\) (56)

**Remark VII.2.** While the explicit structure and dimensions of standard DLAs are generally difficult to classify for arbitrary graph topologies, free DLAs admit full algebraic characterization. Specifically, Theorem 1 of \[17\] provides a complete structural classification of \(\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{free}}\). In particular, if \(\Gamma\) is _archetypal_ (i.e., a

<tbc>connected graph that is neither bipartite nor a cycle), the free DLA is isomorphic to the direct sum of two special unitary Lie algebras:

\(\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{free}}\cong\mathfrak{su}(W_{\Gamma,\mathrm{even}})\oplus\mathfrak{su}(W_{\Gamma,\mathrm{odd}})\cong\mathfrak{su}(2^{n-1})\oplus\mathfrak{su}(2^{n-1}),\) (57)

where _n_=|_V_| is the order of \(\Gamma\), and \(W_{\Gamma,\mathrm{even}}\) (resp. \(W_{\Gamma,\mathrm{odd}}\)) denotes the subspace spanned by Hadamard basis states containing an even (resp. odd) number of \(|-\rangle\) factors.

## B. Reduced DLAs for the MaxCut Problem

The MaxCut cost function exhibits a global Z<sub>2</sub> (bit-flip) symmetry that permits fixing the classical state of an arbitrary reference vertex \(v\in V\) (e.g., _x<sub>v</sub>_=0) without altering the maximum cut value, as the full solution set remains reconstructible via bitwise inversion. A comprehensive exposition of the corresponding symmetry-reduced QAOA formulations, including their dynamical Lie algebras, circuit properties, and algebraic structures, is provided in \[29\]; here, we briefly review the relevant setup.

Quantum mechanically, imposing _x<sub>v</sub>_=0 breaks this two-fold degeneracy and projects the _n_-qubit Hilbert space \((\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}\) onto an (_n_-1)-qubit subspace:

## D. Dynamical Lie Algebras for the Grover-Mixer QAOA

The Grover-mixer QAOA (GM-QAOA), introduced in \[4\], replaces standard local mixers with a highly nonlocal mixer Hamiltonian. The algorithm typically starts in a uniform superposition over all feasible configurations F,

\(|\xi\rangle:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{F}|}}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{F}}|x\rangle.\) (72)

The Grover mixer _G<sub>M</sub>_ is defined as the orthogonal projection (up to a negative sign) onto this initial state:

\(G_M:=-|\xi\rangle\left\langle\xi\right|.\) (73)

Let _d_ denote the number of distinct values attained by the objective function _F_ over F. For each \(j\in\{1,\dots,d\}\), let \(\mathcal{F}_j\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) be the _j_-th level set of _F_, and define the normalized level-set state

\(|\xi_j\rangle:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{F}_j|}}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{F}_j}|x\rangle.\) (74)

As established in \[31, Section V\], the quantum evolution under GM-QAOA remains strictly confined to the _d_-dimensional invariant subspace \(W_0\subseteq W\) spanned by these level-set states:

\(W_0:=\mathrm{span}\big\{|\xi_1\rangle,\dots,|\xi_d\rangle\big\}.\) (75)

Restricting both the mixer _G<sub>M</sub>_ and the problem Hamiltonian _H<sub>P</sub>_ to _W_<sub>0</sub>, we obtain the associated dynamical Lie algebra

\(\mathfrak{g}_\xi:=\left\langle iG_M\right|_{W_0},iH_P\big|_{W_0}\right\rangle_\mathrm{Lie}.\) (76)

Theorem III.1 of \[31\] shows that \(\mathfrak{g}_\xi\) is the full unitary algebra on this subspace:

\(\mathfrak{g}_\xi\cong\mathfrak{u}(W_0)\cong\mathfrak{u}(d).\) (77)

Consequently, GM-QAOA is fully controllable on _W_<sub>0</sub>, whose dimension equals the number _d_ of distinct objective-function values on the feasible set.

Translating this gate-level decomposition into our framework allows us to bound global unitary and state- to-state transition depths directly in terms of the primitive native implementation costs for single-qubit gates (_K_<sub>1q</sub>) and CNOT gates (_K_<sub>CX</sub>).

Next, we specialize the preceding circuit-level synthesis results to the setting where the dynamical Lie algebra is generated by a finite collection of imaginary Pauli strings. This bridges the abstract bounds with explicit, constructive gate sequences implementable within variational quantum algorithms.

**Theorem VIII.5.** Let \(W=(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes n}\) be a qubit Hilbert space with _N_=dim(_W_)=2_<sup>n</sup>_, and suppose that the dynamical Lie algebra<tbc>

Furthermore, the following global bounds hold:

1. Any unitary operator _U_ on _W_ (or \(U\in\mathrm{SU}(W)\) when \(\mathfrak{g}\simeq\mathfrak{su}(W)\)) can be synthesized with a global depth _L_<sub>glob</sub> bounded by<tbc>

\(L_\mathrm{glob}\le 3(2\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}-1)\left(\frac{7}{4}\cdot 4^n-3\cdot 2^{n-1}\right).\) \(\text{(92)}\)

2. Any pair of normalized states \(|\psi\rangle,|\phi\rangle\in W\) can be connected, up to a global phase, with a circuit depth _L_<sub>state</sub> bounded by<tbc>

\(L_\mathrm{state}\le 12(2\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}-1)\left(2^{n+1}-n-2\right).\) \(\text{(93)}\)

Thus the reduced space carries _q=n_-1 logical qubits, and Theorem VIII.5 provides the explicit upper bounds:

\(L_\mathrm{state}\le 12(4n-3)\left(2^n-n-1\right).\) (95)

**Remark VIII.7.** Unlike their unreduced counterparts, symmetry-reduced free MaxCut QAOA instances often achieve full special-unitary, and hence projective operator, controllability on the reduced Hilbert space. ## D. Global Synthesis for Free Flip-or-Stay MIS QAOA

In this subsection, we apply the orbit-generation bounds from Theorem VIII.2 to the free DLA for MIS QAOA on a connected graph \(\Gamma=(V,E)\), obtaining concrete global bounds on circuit synthesis.

We retain the notation established in Section VIIC. However, rather than working directly with the restricted free DLA \(\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{free},\mathcal{F}}\) from (70), we analyze the closely related algebra

\(\widehat{\mathfrak{g}}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{free},\mathcal{F}}:=\left\langle\left\{i\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\right|_{W_\mathcal{F}},iZ_v\right|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\right\}_{v\in V}\right\rangle_\mathrm{Lie},\) (96)

where \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\) denotes the restriction of the local controlled-X mixer operator to the feasible subspace _W_<sub>F</sub>. The action of \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\) on a computational basis state \(|x\rangle\) (for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\)) is given by

\(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}|x\rangle:=H_{CX,v}|x\rangle+(I-\mathcal{P}_v)|x\rangle=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
|x^{(v)}\rangle, & \text{if}x_w=0\text{for all}w\in\mathcal{N}_v, \\
|x\rangle, & \text{if}x_w=1\text{for some}w\in\mathcal{N}_v,
\end{array}\right.\) (97)

where _x_<sup>(_v_)</sup> denotes the bitstring _x_ with the _v_-th bit flipped (cf. (68) and (69)). As shown in \[30, Theorem IV.2\], this modification still results in the generation of the full unitary algebra:

\(\widehat{\mathfrak{g}}_{\Gamma,\mathrm{free},\mathcal{F}}\cong\mathfrak{u}(W_\mathcal{F}).\) (98)

Throughout this subsection, _native pulse_ refers to the Flip-or-Stay control family

\(\widehat{\mathfrak{a}}_\mathrm{MIS}:=\left\{i\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}},iZ_v\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\big|v\in V\right\}.\)

Thus the bounds below are stated in the hatted Flip-or-Stay pulse alphabet.

We next observe that each local mixer stabilizes the set F of feasible bitstrings, thereby inducing a well- defined combinatorial action directly on F. Specifically, for each vertex \(v\in V\) , the local mixer defines a set-theoretic toggle map \(\tau_v:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}\) given by

\(\tau_v(x):=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
x^{(v)}, & \text{if}x_w=0\text{for all}w\in\mathcal{N}_v, \\
x, & \text{if}x_w=1\text{for some}w\in\mathcal{N}_v.
\end{array}\right.\) (99)

As \(\tau_v\) either leaves a bitstring \(x\in\mathcal{F}\) invariant or swaps an isolated pair \(x\leftrightarrow x^{(v)}\), each \(\tau_v\) acts as an involution on the feasible set F:

\(\tau_v^2=\mathrm{id}_\mathcal{F}\text{for all}v\in V.\) (100)

The collection of these local toggles generates a permutation subgroup of the symmetric group Sym(F), known as the _independent-set toggle group_:

\(\mathcal{T}(\Gamma):=\langle\tau_v\rangle_{v\in V}\subseteq\mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{F}).\) (101)

Importantly, the involutory nature of \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\) (see (100)) implies that exponentiating the local mixer flow at parameter \(t=\pi/2\) yields

\(e^{i\frac{\pi}{2}\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}}=\mathrm{cos}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)I_{W_\mathcal{F}}+i\mathrm{sin}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}=i\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}.\) (102)

Thus, up to an overall global phase factor _i_, executing the action of a single discrete toggle permutation \(\tau_v\) on _W_<sub>F</sub> requires exactly one native continuous pulse evolution under the Hamiltonian \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\).

To quantify the pulse complexity of synthesizing arbitrary permutations within the toggle group \(\mathcal{T}(\Gamma):=\langle\tau_v\rangle_{v\in V}\subseteq\mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{F})\), we define the toggle group diameter \(\Delta_\Gamma\) as the diameter of its Cayley graph with respect to the generating set in (101):

\(\Delta_\Gamma:=\mathrm{diamCay}\big(\mathcal{T}(\Gamma),\{\tau_v|v\in V\}\big).\) (103)

<tbc>Consequently, every permutation \(g\in\mathcal{T}(\Gamma)\) admits a word decomposition \(g=\tau_{v_k}\cdots\tau_{v_1}\) of length \(k\le\Delta_\Gamma\). On the Hilbert space _W_<sub>F</sub>, the corresponding unitary operator \(\widehat{g}\in\mathrm{U}(W_\mathcal{F})\) is synthesized as

\(\widehat{g}=\widehat{H}_{CX,v_k}\cdots\widehat{H}_{CX,v_1}=e^{-i\frac{k\pi}{2}}\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{i\frac{\pi}{2}\widehat{H}_{CX,v_k-j}},\) (104)

yielding a continuous mixer circuit implementation with native pulse depth not exceeding \(\Delta_\Gamma\).

**Theorem VIII.8.** Let \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) be a connected graph with feasible independent-set subspace _W_<sub>F</sub> of dimension \(D=|\mathcal{F}|\ge 4\), and let \(\Delta_\Gamma\) denote the toggle group diameter defined in (103). Then:

1. Every unitary \(U\in\mathrm{U}(W_\mathcal{F})\) admits an exact native Flip-or-Stay pulse synthesis with total depth \(L_\mathrm{glob}(\Gamma)\) bounded by<tbc>

\(L_\mathrm{glob}(\Gamma)\le\Delta_\Gamma(D-1)(4D^2-3D+2)+2D^3-D^2.\) \(\text{(105)}\)

2. For any pair of normalized quantum states \(|\psi\rangle,|\phi\rangle\in W_\mathcal{F}\), there exists a native continuous pulse circuit connecting \(|\psi\rangle\) to \(|\phi\rangle\) (up to a global phase) with total depth \(L_\mathrm{state}(\Gamma)\) bounded by<tbc>

\(L_\mathrm{state}(\Gamma)\le 12D^2\Delta_\Gamma+6D^2-16D\Delta_\Gamma+4\Delta_\Gamma-4.\) \(\text{(106)}\)

In particular, as functions of the feasible dimension _D_=|F| and toggle diameter \(\Delta_\Gamma\), the global depth complexities satisfy the asymptotic upper bounds:

\(L_\mathrm{glob}(\Gamma)=\mathcal{O}\left(D^3\Delta_\Gamma\right),L_\mathrm{state}(\Gamma)=\mathcal{O}\left(D^2\Delta_\Gamma\right).\) \(\text{(107)}\)

**Remark VIII.9.** It is instructive to compare these global bounds with the local-vicinity depth complexities summarized in  IV. Specifically, while global unitary and state-to-state synthesis scale as \(\mathcal{O}(D^3\Delta_\Gamma)\) and \(\mathcal{O}(D^2\Delta_\Gamma)\), respectively, local synthesis bounds are governed by the DLA stabilization depth and orbit dimensions--such as O(D**<sub>a</sub>**_D_<sup>2</sup>) for local unitaries and \(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{a},\psi} m_\psi)\) for local states. This trade-off underscores how global pulse schedules incorporate an explicit topological dependence on the toggle group diameter \(\Delta_\Gamma\).

To see how these theoretical bounds manifest in a concrete setting, we next analyze the complete graph family.

**Example VIII.10.** Let \(\Gamma=K_n\) be the complete graph on \(n\ge 3\) vertices. The feasible independent sets consist of the empty set and all singletons:

\(\mathcal{F}(K_n)=\left\{\varnothing,\{1\},\dots,\{n\}\right\},D:=|\mathcal{F}(K_n)|=n+1.\) \(\text{(108)}\)

Identifying the empty set \(\varnothing\) with the symbol 0 and each singleton {_v_} with the symbol \(v\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), the feasible set maps bijectively to {0,1_,...,n_}.

In the complete graph _K<sub>n</sub>_, for any vertex \(v\in V(K_n)\), every independent set distinct from \(\varnothing\) and {_v_} contains a vertex adjacent to _v_. Therefore, the toggle group element \(\tau_v\) associated with vertex _v_ acts as a simple transposition that swaps the empty set, encoded by 0, with the singleton set, encoded by _v_:

\(\tau_v=(0v)\in\mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{F}(K_n)),1\le v\le n.\) \(\text{(109)}\)

Consequently, the independent-set toggle group is generated by the following transpositions:

\(\mathcal{T}(K_n)=\left\langle(01),(02),\dots,(0n)\right\rangle\cong S_{n+1}.\) \(\text{(110)}\)

The corresponding toggle Cayley graph

\(\mathrm{Cay}\left(\mathcal{T}(K_n),\{\tau_1,\dots,\tau_n\}\right)\cong\mathrm{ST}_{n+1}\) \(\text{(111)}\)

is the classical star graph ST<sub>_n_+1</sub> on _n_+1 symbols. By a well-known result of Akers and Krishnamurthy \[2, Theorem 7\], the exact diameter of the star graph ST<sub>_n_+1</sub> is

\(\Delta_{K_n}=\left\lfloor\frac{3(n+1-1)}{2}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{2}\right\rfloor=\mathcal{O}(n).\) \(\text{(112)}\)

Substituting _D=n_+1 and \(\Delta_{K_n}=\mathcal{O}(n)\) into Theorem VIII.8 yields the following explicit polynomial circuit-depth scaling for free MIS QAOA on complete graphs:

\(L_\mathrm{glob}(K_n)=\mathcal{O}(n^4),L_\mathrm{state}(K_n)=\mathcal{O}(n^3).\) \(\text{(113)}\)

## IX. FINITE-DEPTH EXPOSURE OF DESCENT DIRECTIONS

The finite-depth preparation results established in the preceding sections guarantee the existence of parametrized circuits that reproduce elements within a neighborhood \(\mathcal{V}_{[\psi]}\) of a ray \([\psi]\) in the projective orbit \(\mathcal{O}_{[\psi]}\) (see Theorem VI.6). However, they do not provide an explicit mechanism for determining concrete parameter values that realize specific states in this neighborhood. In this section, we take a first step toward resolving this constructive problem by connecting parameter identification to the infinitesimal framework developed in Section VI. Specifically, we show that any finite-depth circuit preparing a non-optimal state can be augmented by a bounded-length identity block, ensuring that the expanded parametrization explicitly exhibits either a first-order descent direction for the loss function or a direction of negative curvature.

Before presenting our main result, we formalize the framework for circuit extensions. Let \(|\xi\rangle\) be an initial reference state, and let

\(\rho_p=|\psi(\theta_p)\rangle\langle\psi(\theta_p)|\) (114)

be the density matrix corresponding to the state \(|\psi(\theta_p)\rangle=U(\theta_p)|\xi\rangle\) prepared by a depth-_p_ parameterized quantum circuit \(U(\theta_p)\). Throughout the remainder of this section, we assume that the observable (problem Hamiltonian) _H<sub>P</sub>_ satisfies \(iH_P\in\mathfrak{g}\), where g is the dynamical Lie algebra, and that the associated Lie group _G_=exp(g) is compact.

An _identity block V_(**_x_**) is a parameterized unitary operation satisfying _V_(**0**)=_I_, generated by a sequence of at most T<sub>g</sub> elementary evolutions under generators of g. Appending _V_(**_x_**) yields the augmented loss function

\(\ell(x,\theta_p):=\mathrm{Tr}\big[V(x)\rho_pV^\dagger(x)H_P\big],\) (115)

which recovers the baseline energy at the origin: \(\ell(0,\theta_p)=\ell(\theta_p)\).

The theorem below formalizes the finite-depth exposure guarantee for arbitrary non-optimal states. For complete derivations and technical proofs, we refer the reader to Appendix E.

**Theorem IX.1** (Finite-depth exposure of descent directions)**.** Assume that the _G_-orbit \(\mathcal{O}_\psi\) of the initial state \(|\psi\rangle\) intersects the ground eigenspace of _H<sub>P</sub>_, and suppose the energy prepared by the current circuit is strictly non-optimal:

\(\ell_{\theta_p}(\rho,H_P)>\lambda_\mathrm{min}(H_P),\)

where \(\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\) is the initial state density matrix and \(\ell_{\theta_p}(\rho,H_P)=\mathrm{Tr}\big[U(\theta_p)\rho U^\dagger(\theta_p)H_P\big]\) denotes the current expectation value. Then, there exists an identity block _V_(**_x_**) requiring at most T<sub>g</sub> elementary generator evolutions such that after appending _V_(**_x_**), exactly one of the following holds for the augmented loss function \(\ell_{(x,\theta_p)}(\rho,H_P)\) associated with the extended unitary \(U(x,\theta_p)=V(x)U(\theta_p)\):

1. **First-Order Descent:** The parameter gradient at the origin is non-vanishing,<tbc>

\(\nabla_x\ell_{(x,\theta_p)}(\rho,H_P)\big|_{x=0}\neq 0.\) \(\text{(116)}\)

2. **Second-Order Escape:** The gradient vanishes at **_x_**=**0**, but there exists a direction \(v\in\mathbb{R}^m\) exhibiting negative second-order curvature:<tbc>

\(\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\big|_{t=0}\ell_{(tv,\theta_p)}(\rho,H_P)<0.\) \(\text{(117)}\)

Consequently, every neighborhood of **0** contains parameters **_x_** yielding strict energy improvement:

\(\ell_{(x,\theta_p)}(\rho,H_P)<\ell_{\theta_p}(\rho,H_P).\) \(\text{(118)}\)

The identity block extension requires at most T<sub>g</sub> elementary generator evolutions.

**Remark IX.2** (Computational complexity of the escape block)**.** Recall that the identity block depth satisfies \(\mathcal{T}_\mathbf{a}=\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{D}_\mathbf{a}\mathrm{dim}\mathfrak{g})\le\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{dim}(\mathfrak{g})^2)\) (see Theorem VI.4), where D<sub>**a**</sub> is the filtration depth of the generator pool. Consequently, for Lie-algebraic architectures with polynomially bounded DLA dimension dim(g)=poly(_n_), Theorem IX.1 guarantees that any suboptimal stationary point can be escaped by appending a local identity block of depth at most poly(_n_).

### A. Relation to Existing Landscape and Circuit Extension Results

Theorem IX.1 connects naturally to existing strategies for escaping local minima in Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm landscapes, adaptive control architectures, and quantum optimization theory.

**Comparison with QAOA Layer-Extension Frameworks.** A prominent approach to breaking out of suboptimal stationary points involves inserting additional gates into an existing circuit. Sack, Medina, Kueng, and Serbyn \[24\] start from a local minimum of a depth-_p_ QAOA circuit energy function and insert two zero-angle gates in 2_p_+1 prescribed ways. The resulting depth-(_p_+1) circuits prepare the same state and act as stationary points of the enlarged loss function. When the enlarged Hessians are non-degenerate, each of these 2_p_+1 stationary points possesses exactly one negative Hessian eigenvalue, exposing a direction of strict energy improvement \[24, Theorems 1,2\]. Medina and Serbyn \[21\] subsequently refined this mechanism by constructing an explicit escape vector without needing Hessian diagonalization \[21, Sec. III.A\].

**Key Distinctions and Generality.** While sharing the operational intuition of identity-initialized circuit extensions (_V_(**0**)=_I_), Theorem IX.1 extends beyond these QAOA-specific results in several fundamental ways:

1. **Generality of States and Architectures.** Theorem IX.1 places no structural restrictions on the baseline ansatz \(U(\theta_p)\) and applies to _any_ reachable state \(\rho_p\) satisfying \(\ell_{\theta_p}(\rho_p,H_P)>\lambda_{min}(H_P)\) (i.e., not a global minimum). It does not require the baseline parameters \(\theta_p\) to form a non-degenerate local minimum; the conclusion also covers arbitrary stationary points, thereby guaranteeing that no suboptimal stationary state traps the optimization process at finite depth.<tbc>

2. **Local Parameter Isolation.** Strict local improvement \(\ell_{(x,\theta_p)}(\rho,H_P)<\ell_{\theta_p}(\rho,H_P)\) is achieved by varying _only_ the newly appended parameters **_x_** near **0**, leaving the trained baseline parameters \(\theta_p\) entirely untouched.<tbc>
