## X. SUMMARY AND OUTLOOK

As this work connects quantum control theory, dynamical Lie algebras, orbit geometry, and quantum- circuit synthesis across several variational architectures, we organize the summary around the central questions addressed by our results. This question-and-answer format also clarifies their broader implications and the problems that remain open.

_What is the correct notion of reachability for a variational circuit?_ The accessible states form the dynamical group orbit of the initial state, rather than the entire cyclic invariant subspace generated by the initial state under the DLA action. This distinction can be substantial: an orbit of only polynomial dimension may contain exponentially many linearly independent optima. Orbit geometry therefore provides both the appropriate reachability criterion and a precise description of its limitations.

_When does asymptotic reachability imply exact finite-depth preparation?_ We show that this implication holds whenever the relevant projective orbit is closed. In particular, a nondegenerate eigenstate of one of the initial control operators has a closed projective orbit even when the full dynamical group is not closed inside the ambient unitary group. For QAOA employing an irreducible stoquastic mixer, this converts asymptotic convergence into exact ground state preparation at some finite depth.

_Which circuit depth is sufficient?_ Locally, the commutator filtration translates the rate at which native controls generate new Lie-algebra and orbit directions into explicit bounds on the required number of native pulses. Globally, when the restricted DLA is full or special unitary, we develop complementary constructions based on diagonal and two-level synthesis, alongside logical-gate compilation. The Pauli-generated DLA case links these global costs directly to the filtration depth, whereas the MIS toggle construction provides a fully explicit realization from the original controls. Together, these results elevate qualitative controllability into quantitative resource guarantees, while clearly distinguishing the cost of arbitrary unitary synthesis from the typically more efficient state-to-state transfer.

<tbc>_What are the implications for variational optimization?_ Under the stated compactness and reachable-ground state assumptions, the local synthesis construction produces a bounded-depth, identity-initialized circuit extension block that exposes either first-order descent or a negative-curvature direction at every suboptimal circuit output. Thus, the algebra and geometry of the reachable orbit constrain not only expressivity but also the local optimization landscape.

_What remains open?_ The principal questions are quantitative and algorithmic: how tight the depth bounds are, how large the local synthesis neighborhoods can be chosen, and how the required circuit parameters can be found efficiently. Incorporating hardware connectivity, locality, and noise may lead to substantially sharper architecture-dependent bounds. Resolving these questions would bring the structural guarantees developed here closer to practical finite-depth circuit design and optimization.

\(B_P:=Z_v|_{W_\mathcal{F}}-\widehat{P}Z_v|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\widehat{P}^\dagger=Z_{v,0}-\widehat{P}Z_{v,0}\widehat{P}^\dagger,\) (D8)

<tbc>and define the real linear span

\(\mathcal{E}_v:=\mathrm{span}_\mathbb{R}\{B_P|P\in\mathcal{T}(\Gamma)\}\subseteq\mathfrak{d}_0(W_\mathcal{F}),\) (D9)

where \(\mathfrak{d}_0(W_\mathcal{F})\cong\mathbb{R}^{D-1}\) denotes the space of all traceless diagonal Hermitian operators on _W_<sub>F</sub>.

By a result of Striker \[28, Corollary 3.24\], for every connected graph \(\Gamma\), the toggle group satisfies

\(A_\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{T}(\Gamma)\subseteq\mathrm{Sym}(\mathcal{F}),\) (D10)

where _A_<sub>F</sub> and Sym(F) denote the alternating and symmetric groups on F, respectively.

For every \(Q\in\mathcal{T}(\Gamma)\), one has

\(\widehat{Q}B_P\widehat{Q}^\dagger=B_{QP}-B_Q\in E_v,\)

which proves that _E<sub>v</sub>_ is a \(\mathcal{T}(\Gamma)\)-invariant subspace (subrepresentation) of d<sub>0</sub>(_W_<sub>F</sub>).

To show that _E<sub>v</sub>_=d<sub>0</sub>(_W_<sub>F</sub>), first note that \(E_v\neq\{0\}\): the diagonal operator _Z_<sub>_v,_0</sub> is nonconstant because the feasible configurations \(\varnothing\) and {_v_} have opposite _Z<sub>v</sub>_-eigenvalues, and the transitive action of \(\mathcal{T}(\Gamma)\) cannot fix a nonconstant diagonal vector. Since the subspace d<sub>0</sub>(_W_<sub>F</sub>) is isomorphic to the standard real representation

<tbc>of _A<sub>D</sub>_ (where _D_=|F|), and this representation is irreducible for all \(D\ge 4\), it follows that the subspace E_<sub>v</sub>_ generated by orbit differences coincides with the entire space:<tbc>

\(E_v=\mathfrak{d}_0(W_\mathcal{F}).\)

<tbc>We can therefore select _D_-1 permutations \(P_1,\dots,P_{D-1}\in\mathcal{T}(\Gamma)\) such that {_B_<sub>_P_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,B_<sub>_P_<sub>_D_-1</sub></sub>} forms a basis for d<sub>0</sub>(_W_<sub>F</sub>). Since \(\mathrm{Tr}_{W_\mathcal{F}}(Z_v)\neq 0\), appending _Z<sub>v</sub>_|<sub>_W_<sub>F</sub></sub> yields a full basis for all diagonal Hermitian operators \(\mathfrak{d}(W_\mathcal{F})\cong\mathbb{R}^D\):

\(\mathrm{span}_\mathbb{R}\left\{Z_v|_{W_\mathcal{F}},B_{P_1},\dots,B_{P_{D-1}}\right\}=\mathfrak{d}(W_\mathcal{F}).\) (D11)

Thus, any diagonal Hamiltonian \(H\in\mathfrak{d}(W_\mathcal{F})\) expands uniquely as<tbc>

\(H=c_0Z_v|_{W_\mathcal{F}}+\sum_{k=1}^{D-1}c_k\big(Z_v|_{W_\mathcal{F}}-\widehat{P}_kZ_v|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\widehat{P}_k^\dagger\big),c_0,c_1,\dots,c_{D-1}\in\mathbb{R}.\) (D12)

<tbc>Since all diagonal operators mutually commute, exponentiating Eq. (D12) yields an exact product factorization for an arbitrary diagonal unitary _e<sup>itH</sup>_:

\(e^{itH}=e^{it\big(c_0+\sum_{k=1}^{D-1}c_k\big)Z_v|_{W_\mathcal{F}}}\cdot\prod_{k=1}^{D-1}\widehat{P}_ke^{-itc_kZ_v|_{W_\mathcal{F}}}\widehat{P}_k^\dagger,t\in\mathbb{R}.\) (D13)

Although a native toggle word realizes \(\widehat{P}_k\) only up to an overall phase, this phase factor cancels out identically under conjugation, ensuring that the phase ambiguity of the toggle implementation does not affect the exactness of the diagonal factorization in (D13).

By (103), each unitary permutation operator \(\widehat{P}_k\) is implementable (up to a global phase) to depth at most \(\Delta_\Gamma\) using native mixer pulses. Each conjugated factor \(\widehat{P}_ke^{-itc_kZ_v}\widehat{P}_k^\dagger\) therefore requires at most \(2\Delta_\Gamma+1\) native operations (1 diagonal pulse drive under _Z<sub>v</sub>_ surrounded by 2 toggle sub-circuits of depth \(\Delta_\Gamma\)). Combining these with the single un-conjugated _Z<sub>v</sub>_ pulse gives a bound on the exact diagonal synthesis complexity.

**Proposition D.1.** Let \(\Gamma\) be a connected graph with \(D=|\mathcal{F}|\ge 4\). Every diagonal unitary operator \(U_\mathrm{diag}\in\mathrm{U}(W_\mathcal{F})\) (including its global phase) can be synthesized exactly using at most

\(K_\mathrm{diag}\le 1+(D-1)(2\Delta_\Gamma+1)\) (D14)

native pulse operations.

## b. Extraction of Single Two-Level Matrix Units

Having established exact diagonal synthesis, we now show how to isolate an individual two-level matrix unit _X<sub>rs</sub>_ with \(r,s\in\mathcal{F}\) (see (79)).

Fix a vertex \(v\in V\) . Because \(\tau_v\) acts as a set-theoretic involution on F, its action on the basis of _W_<sub>F</sub> decomposes into a disjoint union of transpositions and fixed points:

\(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}=Q_v+\sum_{\{r,s\}\in M_v}X_{rs},X_{rs}:=|r\rangle\langle s|+|s\rangle\langle r|,\) (D15)

where _M<sub>v</sub>_ is a non-empty matching of feasible strings transposed by \(\tau_v\), and \(Q_v:=\sum_{w\in\mathrm{Fix}(\tau_v)}|w\rangle\langle w|\) is the diagonal projector onto the fixed subspace of \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\).

Consider a pair of strings \(\{a,b\}\in M_v\) swapped by \(\tau_v\). Because the edges of the matching _M<sub>v</sub>_ are pairwise disjoint, we can construct a diagonal sign operator \(S\in\mathrm{U}(W_\mathcal{F})\):

\(S:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{F}}\varepsilon_x|x\rangle\langle x|,\varepsilon_x\in\{\pm 1\},\) (D16)

<tbc>such that the pair signs satisfy<tbc>

\(\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_b=+1,\text{and}\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_s=-1\text{for every}\{r,s\}\in M_v\backslash\{\{a,b\}\}.\) (D17)

<tbc>Since _S=S_<sup>†</sup>=_S_<sup>-1</sup>, conjugating _X<sub>rs</sub>_ by _S_ yields \(SX_{rs}S^{-1}=\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_sX_{rs}\). Applied to \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\), this sign assignment flips the direction of every matching term except the target _X<sub>ab</sub>_:<tbc>

\(S\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}S^{-1}=Q_v+X_{ab}-\sum_{\{r,s\}\in M_v\backslash\{\{a,b\}\}}X_{rs}.\) (D18)

<tbc>Averaging \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\) with its conjugated counterpart yields<tbc>

\(\frac{1}{2}\left(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}+S\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}S^{-1}\right)=Q_v+X_{ab}.\) (D19)

<tbc>Crucially, the operators \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\) and \(S\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}S^{-1}\) commute. Indeed, both are block-diagonal with respect to the orthogonal decomposition<tbc>

\(W_\mathcal{F}=\oplus_{w\in\mathrm{Fix}(\tau_v)}\mathrm{span}_\mathbb{C}\{|w\rangle\}\oplus\oplus_{\{r,s\}\in M_v}\mathrm{span}_\mathbb{C}\{|r\rangle,|s\rangle\}.\) (D20)

<tbc>On each two-dimensional matching subspace \(\mathrm{span}_\mathbb{C}\{|r\rangle,|s\rangle\}\), \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}\) restricts to the Pauli-_X_ matrix, while \(S\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}S^{-1}\) restricts to either +_X_ (on {_a,b_}) or -_X_ (on _M<sub>v</sub>_\\{{_a,b_}}). Because _X_ commutes with \(\pm X\), the sum-of-generators exponentiates to a product of commuting unitaries:<tbc>

\(e^{-i\frac{t}{2}\widehat{H}_{CX,v}}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}e^{-i\frac{t}{2}S\widehat{H}_{CX,v}}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}S^{-1}=e^{-it(Q_v+X_{ab})}.\) (D21)

<tbc>As the diagonal projector _Q<sub>v</sub>_ and the off-diagonal generator _X<sub>ab</sub>_ have disjoint support on _W_<sub>F</sub>, they commute (\[_Q<sub>v</sub>,X<sub>ab</sub>_\]=0). We can therefore isolate the target two-level flow _e_<sup>-_itX<sub>ab</sub>_</sup> as

\(e^{-itX_{ab}}=e^{itQ_v}e^{-i\frac{t}{2}\widehat{H}_{CX,v}}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}Se^{-i\frac{t}{2}\widehat{H}_{CX,v}}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}S^{-1},\) (D22)

where we used the identity \(e^{-i\frac{t}{2}S\widehat{H}_{CX,v}}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}S^{-1}=Se^{-i\frac{t}{2}\widehat{H}_{CX,v}}\big|_{W_\mathcal{F}}S^{-1}\).

**Proposition D.2.** Let \(\Gamma=(V,E)\) be a connected graph with \(D=|\mathcal{F}|\ge 4\). For any vertex \(v\in V\) and every toggle edge \(\{a,b\}\in M_v\), the two-level flow \(e^{-itX_{ab}}(t\in\mathbb{R})\) can be synthesized exactly using at most

\(K_X^{(v)}\le 3K_\mathrm{diag}+2\le 6\Delta_\Gamma D+3D-6\Delta_\Gamma+2\) (D23)

native pulses.

Consequently, for any pair of distinct feasible configurations \(r,s\in\mathcal{F}\), the corresponding two-level flow _e_<sup>-_itX<sub>rs</sub>_</sup> can be synthesized exactly using at most

\(K_X\le K_X^{(v)}+2\Delta_\Gamma\le 3K_\mathrm{diag}+2+2\Delta_\Gamma\le 6\Delta_\Gamma D+3D-4\Delta_\Gamma+2\) (D24)

native pulses.

_Proof._ Fix \(v\in V\) and a toggle edge \(\{a,b\}\in M_v\). We employ the realization of _e_<sup>-_itX<sub>ab</sub>_</sup> from (D22). The diagonal unitary _e<sup>itQ<sub>v</sub>_</sup> requires at most _K_<sub>diag</sub> native pulses. Each of the two evolutions under \(\widehat{H}_{CX,v}\) requires one native mixer pulse, while _S_ and _S_<sup>-1</sup> each require at most _K_<sub>diag</sub> pulses. Therefore,

\(K_X^{(v)}\le K_\mathrm{diag}+1+K_\mathrm{diag}+1+K_\mathrm{diag}=3K_\mathrm{diag}+2.\)

Substituting the upper bound for _K_<sub>diag</sub> from (D14) yields the bound in (D23).

Now let \(r,s\in\mathcal{F}\) be distinct feasible bitstrings. By (D10), the toggle group contains the alternating group:

\(\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{T}(\Gamma).\)

<tbc>Since \(D\ge 4\), the alternating group A<sub>F</sub> acts transitively on ordered pairs of distinct elements in F. Hence, there exists a permutation \(P\in\mathcal{T}(\Gamma)\) such that<tbc>

\(P(a)=r,P(b)=s.\)

<tbc>Denoting by \(\widehat{P}\in U(W_\mathcal{F})\) the corresponding permutation operator, we obtain<tbc>

\(\widehat{P}X_{ab}\widehat{P}^{-1}=X_{rs},\)

<tbc>and consequently,

\(e^{-itX_{rs}}=\widehat{P}e^{-itX_{ab}}\widehat{P}^{-1}.\) (D25)

By definition of the toggle-group diameter \(\Delta_\Gamma\), both \(\widehat{P}\) and \(\widehat{P}^{-1}\) can be implemented using at most \(\Delta_\Gamma\) local mixer generators. It follows that

\(K_X\le K_X^{(v)}+2\Delta_\Gamma.\)

Combining this inequality with (D23) yields (D24).

By substituting the explicit primitive costs _K<sub>X</sub>_ (Proposition D.2) and _K_<sub>diag</sub> (Proposition D.1) into the general pulse-complexity bounds of Eq. (86) and Theorem VIII.2, we establish the global synthesis and state-to-state transition bounds asserted in Theorem VIII.8.

## Appendix E: Finite-Depth Exposure of Descent Directions: Detailed Treatment

Let \(\mathfrak{g}\subseteq\mathfrak{u}(W)\) be the dynamical Lie algebra generated by the available skew-Hermitian control operators, and let _G_ denote the associated connected dynamical Lie group. We assume that the problem Hamiltonian satisfies \(iH_P\in\mathfrak{g}\). Working in the density operator formalism eliminates unphysical global phase ambiguities; we further assume that _G_ is a compact Lie group.

For a normalized initial state \(|\xi\rangle\), we recall that \(\rho=|\xi\rangle\langle\xi|\) is the initial density matrix. The corresponding _reachable state orbit_ under _G_ is the adjoint orbit

\(\mathcal{O}_\rho:=\{g\rho g^\dagger:g\in G\}.\) (E1)

A parameterized quantum circuit specifies a smooth map \(U(\theta)\in G\), which induces the circuit state endpoint map<tbc>

\(\Phi_\rho(\theta):=U(\theta)\rho U^\dagger(\theta)\in\mathcal{O}_\rho.\)

<tbc>The circuit loss function measures the expectation value of the problem Hamiltonian _H<sub>P</sub>_:

\(\ell_\theta(\rho,H_P):=\langle\psi(\theta)|H_P|\psi(\theta)\rangle=\text{Tr}\big(H_PU(\theta)\rho U^\dagger(\theta)\big),\) (E2)

where \(|\psi(\theta)\rangle=U(\theta)|\xi\rangle\). The loss function factors through the state orbit as the composition<tbc>

\(\ell_\theta(\rho,H_P)=(h\circ\Phi_\rho)(\theta),\)

<tbc>where \(h:\mathcal{O}_\rho\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is the linear height function defined by

\(h(A):=\text{Tr}(H_P\cdot A).\) (E3)

## 1. The loss landscape on the reachable orbit

**Proposition E.1** (Absence of suboptimal orbit minima)**.** Assume that the adjoint orbit \(\mathcal{O}_\rho\) of a pure-state projector \(\rho\) (see (E1)) contains a projector \(|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|\) onto a normalized ground state of _H<sub>P</sub>_:

\(\mathrm{min}_{A\in\mathcal{O}_\rho} h(A)=\langle\phi|H_P|\phi\rangle=\lambda_\mathrm{min}(H_P).\) (E4)

Then _h_ has no suboptimal local minima on \(\mathcal{O}_\rho\). Specifically:

(i) Every local minimum \(A\in\mathcal{O}_\rho\) is a global minimum, corresponding to a rank-one projector onto a ground state of _H<sub>P</sub>_ with \(h(A)=\lambda_\mathrm{min}(H_P)\).<tbc>

(ii) Every critical point \(A\in\mathcal{O}_\rho\) with \(h(A)>\lambda_\mathrm{min}(H_P)\) possesses a tangent direction \(Y\in T_A\mathcal{O}_\rho\) of strictly negative second variation:<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Hess}(h|_{\mathcal{O}_\rho})_A(Y,Y)<0.\) (E5)

<tbc>_Proof of Proposition E.1._ Let h=_i_g denote the Hermitian form of the dynamical Lie algebra, and let proj<sub>h</sub> be the Hilbert-Schmidt orthogonal projection onto h. Define the compact connected adjoint orbit<tbc>

\(\mathcal{A}:=\mathrm{Ad}_G\big(\mathrm{proj}_\mathfrak{h}\rho\big)\subset\mathfrak{h}.\)

<tbc>By _G_-equivariance of proj<sub>h</sub> and inclusion of stabilizers \(G_\rho\subseteq G_{\mathrm{proj}_\mathfrak{h}}_\rho\), the map<tbc>

\(q:\mathcal{O}_\rho\longrightarrow\mathcal{A},q(A)=\mathrm{proj}_\mathfrak{h}A,\) (E6)

<tbc>is a well-defined surjective submersion. Because \(H_P\in\mathfrak{h}\), the energy functional factors through _q_ as _h(A_)=_f(q(A_)), where

\(f:\mathcal{A}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R},f(M)=\mathrm{Tr}(MH_P).\) (E7)

The function _f_ is the component of the moment map for the Hamiltonian _G_-action on the orbit A along the line spanned by \(H_P\in\mathfrak{h}\). By \[3, Lemma 2.2\], any such moment-map component is a Morse-Bott function whose critical manifolds all have even Morse indices. Since critical manifolds of index zero correspond to local minima and distinct sublevel set components can merge only at critical manifolds of index one (which are absent here), _f_ possesses a unique local-minimum connected component on A, which is necessarily the global minimum set \[3, Lemma 2.1\]. Because all Morse-Bott indices of _f_ are even, any critical point lying outside this global minimum set cannot have index zero and must instead have index \(\lambda\ge 2\), meaning the Hessian has at least two negative eigenvalues. Consequently, every non-global critical point \(M\in\mathcal{A}\) admits a tangent direction \(Z\in T_M\mathcal{A}\) such that Hess(_f)<sub>M</sub>(Z,Z)\<_0.

As _q_ is a smooth submersion, its differential \(dq_A:T_A\mathcal{O}_\rho\rightarrow T_{q(A)}\mathcal{A}\) is surjective at every point \(A\in\mathcal{O}_\rho\). Pullback by a submersion preserves local minima and critical points \[7, Proposition 9.6\]. If \(A\in\mathcal{O}_\rho\) is a critical point of _h_ with \(h(A)>\lambda_\mathrm{min}(H_P)\), then _q(A_) is a non-global critical point of _f_. Choosing \(Y\in T_A\mathcal{O}_\rho\) such that \(dq_A(Y)=Z\in T_{q(A)}\mathcal{A}\), the second-order chain rule at a critical point (_df_<sub>_q(A_)</sub>=0) yields

\(\mathrm{Hess}(h|_{\mathcal{O}_\rho})_A(Y,Y)=\mathrm{Hess}(f)_{q(A)}(Z,Z)<0.\)

Finally, assumption (E4) identifies the global minimum value on \(\mathcal{O}_\rho\) with \(\lambda_\mathrm{min}(H_P)\), completing the proof.

At a noncritical orbit point \(\sigma\), an explicit loss function descent generator direction is

\(X_\sigma:=\mathrm{proj}_\mathfrak{g}\big([\sigma,H_P]\big),\) (E8)

where the projection uses the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product \(\langle X,Y\rangle_\mathrm{HS}=-\mathrm{Tr}(XY)\) on skew-Hermitian matrices. For the one-parameter unitary flow \(\sigma(t)=e^{tX_\sigma}\sigma e^{-tX_\sigma}\), the corresponding loss function \(\ell_t(\sigma,H_P)=\mathrm{Tr}(H_P\sigma(t))\) satisfies

\(\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\ell_t(\sigma,H_P)=-\|X_\sigma\|_\mathrm{HS}^2<0.\) (E9)

Moreover, \(X_\sigma=0\) if and only if \(\sigma\) is a critical point of the orbit loss under _G_.

## a. Lifting orbit descent to circuit parameters

Let _m_=dim<sub>R</sub>(g) denote the dimension of the dynamical Lie algebra. The construction from Section VI provides a smooth local family of parameterized unitaries

\(V(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{\ell=1}^Le^{\vartheta_\ell(\mathbf{x})a_{j_\ell}},L\le\mathcal{T}_\mathfrak{g},\) (E10)

defined on a neighborhood of \(\mathbf{0}\in\mathbb{R}^m\), where the \(a_{j_\ell}\) are skew-Hermitian control generators and

\(V(\mathbf{0})=I,(dV)_\mathbf{0}(\mathbb{R}^m)=\mathfrak{g}.\) (E11)

Fix a circuit \(U(\unknown_p)\) of depth _p_, and set

\(\rho_p:=U(\unknown_p)\rho U^\dagger(\unknown_p).\)

For the augmented circuit

\(U(\mathbf{x},\unknown_p)=V(\mathbf{x})U(\unknown_p),\) (E12)

the loss function becomes

\(\ell_{(\mathbf{x},\unknown_p)}(\rho,H_P)=\mathrm{Tr}\big[V(\mathbf{x})\rho_pV^\dagger(\mathbf{x})H_P\big].\) (E13)

In particular,

\(\ell_{(\mathbf{0},\unknown_p)}(\rho,H_P)=\ell_{\unknown_p}(\rho,H_P),\) (E14)

demonstrating that appending the identity block initially preserves the state and energy.

_Proof of Theorem IX.1._ Consider the state endpoint map \(\Psi_p:\mathbb{R}^m\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_\rho\) given by

\(\Psi_p(\mathbf{x})=V(\mathbf{x})\rho_pV^\dagger(\mathbf{x}).\)

By virtue of (E11), its differential at the origin satisfies

\((d\Psi_p)_\mathbf{0}(\mathbb{R}^m)=[\mathfrak{g},\rho_p]=T_{\rho_p}\mathcal{O}_\rho.\) (E15)

Thus, \(\Psi_p\) is a local submersion onto the unitary orbit \(\mathcal{O}_\rho\) at **_x_=0**. By \[7, Proposition 9.6\], first- and second-order criticality of the parameterized loss \(\ell_{(\mathbf{x},\unknown_p)}\) at **_x_=0** is strictly equivalent to that of the orbit loss at \(\rho_p\).

Since Proposition E.1 asserts that all non global minima orbit critical points are saddle points or local maxima (excluding suboptimal second-order local minima), \(\rho_p\) cannot be second-order optimal unless \(\ell_{\unknown_p}(\rho,H_P)=\lambda_\mathrm{min}(H_P)\). Thus either the parameter gradient is nonzero or the parameter Hessian has a negative direction. In either case, arbitrarily small parameter changes strictly decrease the loss.
